docs.text: AI Agent = Ek LLM-powered system jo khud decide kar sakta hai ki kya karna hai, kaunsa tool use karna hai, aur kab tak kaam karte rehna hai — bina har step pe human ke bataye.

docs.title: 1. What is an AI Agent
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Agent ek aisa system hai jisme LLM sirf ek static response generate nahi karta, balki: - Situation ko assess karta hai - Decide karta hai kya action lena hai (tool call, search, calculation, etc.) - Action ka result dekhta hai - Result ke hisaab se agla decision leta hai - Yeh loop tab tak chalta hai jab tak task complete na ho jaye

Analogy: Socho ek normal LLM response ek calculator jaisa hai — ek input do, ek output milta hai, bas. Agent ek assistant/employee jaisa hai — usse ek goal do ("yeh report complete karo"), aur wo khud decide karta hai ki kya research karni hai, kaunsa tool use karna hai, kab dobara try karna hai, aur kab kaam "done" maan lena hai.

docs.title: 2. Agent vs Chain — The Core Difference
docs.text:
Yeh sabse important concept hai jo clearly samajhna chahiye:

Feature Chain Agent Flow Fixed, predetermined sequence of steps Dynamic — LLM khud decide karta hai next step kya hoga Decision-Making Developer ne pehle hi decide kar diya hai flow LLM real-time me decide karta hai Predictability ✅ Highly predictable ❌ Less predictable (but more flexible) Example "Retrieve documents → Summarize → Translate" (fixed order, hamesha yehi hoga) "User ka goal poora karo" — LLM khud decide karega ki search karna hai, calculator use karna hai, ya directly answer dena hai Complexity Handling Simple, well-defined tasks ke liye best Complex, open-ended, multi-step tasks ke liye best

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Chain (Fixed Flow):

Input → Retrieve Documents → Summarize → Output

(Hamesha yehi 3 steps honge, chahe query kuch bhi ho)

Agent (Dynamic Flow):

Input: "What's the weather in Tokyo and should I bring an umbrella?"

Agent's Internal Decision Process:
Step 1: "I need current weather data" → decides to call weather_tool
Step 2: Gets weather result → "It's raining"
Step 3: "I now have enough info to answer" → generates final answer

(Agar query different hoti, agent alag tools/steps choose karta — yehi flexibility hai)

One-line distinction: Chain me developer decide karta hai flow kya hoga. Agent me LLM khud decide karta hai flow kya hoga, real-time me.

docs.title: 3. Key Components of an Agent
docs.text: Component Role LLM (Brain) Reasoning aur decision-making karta hai Tools External functions jo agent call kar sakta hai (search, calculator, database, API) Memory Conversation history/context yaad rakhna (agle topic me detail se) Planning Module Complex task ko chhote steps me todna Instructions/System Prompt Agent ka goal, constraints, aur behavior define karta hai

docs.title: 4. The ReAct Pattern (Reasoning + Acting)
docs.text: Simple Meaning: ReAct ek prompting pattern hai jisme model "Thought → Action → Observation" cycle follow karta hai — pehle sochta hai, phir action leta hai, phir result dekhta hai, phir wapas sochta hai.

docs.title: The Cycle
docs.text:
Thought: Mujhe kya karna chahiye is problem ko solve karne ke liye?
Action: [Tool ko call karo]
Observation: [Tool ka result dekho]
Thought: Ab mujhe kya pata chala? Kya aur info chahiye?
Action: [Agar zaroorat ho toh doosra tool call karo]
Observation: [Naya result]
...
Thought: Ab mere paas final answer dene layak info hai.
Final Answer: [Answer do]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Query: "What is the population of the capital of France, divided by 2?"

Thought: I need to find the capital of France first.
Action: search("capital of France")
Observation: "Paris is the capital of France."

Thought: Now I need the population of Paris.
Action: search("population of Paris")
Observation: "Paris has a population of about 2.1 million."

Thought: I now need to divide this by 2.
Action: calculator(2100000 / 2)
Observation: "1,050,000"

Thought: I now have all the information needed.
Final Answer: The population of Paris divided by 2 is approximately 1,050,000.

docs.title: Why ReAct Works Well
docs.text:
• ✅ Model ka reasoning transparent/traceable hota hai — aap dekh sakte ho model kya soch raha hai (debugging aasan).
  • ✅ Complex, multi-step problems ko naturally break karta hai.
  • ✅ Tool use ke saath seamlessly integrate hota hai.

docs.title: 5. Agent Loop — Step-by-Step Execution
docs.text:
Har agent internally ek loop follow karta hai jab tak task complete na ho:

1. Receive Goal/Task
2. Observe current state (context, previous results)
3. Reason/Think — "What should I do next?"
4. Decide — Take an action (call a tool) OR finish with final answer
5. Execute action (if any)
6. Observe result of action
7. Go back to Step 3 (repeat until done)
8. Return final answer

docs.title: Stopping Conditions (Important!)
docs.text: Agent ka loop kab rukega, yeh decide karna zaroori hai: - LLM khud decide kare ki "task complete hai" (natural stopping) - Maximum iteration limit (e.g., "max 10 steps", taaki infinite loop na ho) - Timeout (e.g., "30 seconds se zyada mat lena") - Human intervention/approval milne tak rukna

docs.title: 6. Planning in Agents
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Complex task ko agent chhote, manageable sub-tasks me todta hai, phir unhe ek-ek karke solve karta hai.

docs.title: Planning Approaches
docs.text: Approach Kya Hota Hai Single-Path Planning Agent ek hi plan banata hai aur usko step-by-step execute karta hai Tree-of-Thought Planning Agent multiple possible plans/paths explore karta hai, phir best choose karta hai Re-planning Agar beech me kuch galat ho jaye ya naya info mile, agent apna plan update/revise karta hai

docs.title: Example — Planning Breakdown
docs.text:
Goal: "Write a research report on renewable energy trends in 2026"

Agent's Plan:
1. Search for latest renewable energy statistics
2. Search for major policy changes in 2026
3. Search for key companies/innovations
4. Synthesize findings into structured sections
5. Write introduction and conclusion
6. Compile final report

docs.title: 7. Types of Agents
docs.text: Type Description Simple Reflex Agent Sirf current input ke basis pe react karta hai, koi memory/planning nahi Tool-Using Agent External tools (search, calculator, APIs) call kar sakta hai Planning Agent Complex tasks ko sub-tasks me todkar sequentially solve karta hai Multi-Agent System Multiple specialized agents mil ke ek complex task solve karte hain (agle topics me detail) Autonomous Agent Minimal human supervision ke saath, long-running tasks continuously perform karta hai

docs.title: 8. Agent Architectures Comparison
docs.text: Architecture Best For ReAct General-purpose reasoning + tool use, most common starting point Plan-and-Execute Jab pehle se clear plan banana zaroori ho complex tasks ke liye (plan pehle banate hain, phir execute karte hain, without re-thinking at every single step) Reflexion/Self-Refine Jab agent ko apna output khud review/improve karna ho Multi-Agent (Supervisor) Jab task itna complex ho ki specialized roles (researcher, coder, reviewer) chahiye

docs.title: 9. Challenges with Agents
docs.text: Challenge Description Unpredictability Agent kabhi-kabhi unexpected/wrong path le sakta hai Infinite Loops Agar stopping condition sahi na ho, agent baar-baar same action repeat kar sakta hai Cost Har reasoning step ek LLM call hai — complex tasks me bahut saare calls ho sakte hain (expensive) Latency Multiple steps/tool calls ki wajah se response slow ho sakta hai Error Propagation Agar ek step me galti hui, aage ke saare steps bhi galat ho sakte hain Debugging Difficulty Multi-step dynamic flow ko debug karna chain ke comparison me mushkil hai

docs.title: 10. Real-World Examples
docs.text: Example What the Agent Does Coding Agent (e.g., Claude Code) Code likhta hai, run karta hai, errors dekh ke fix karta hai, dobara test karta hai Research Agent Multiple sources search karta hai, information synthesize karta hai, report banata hai Customer Support Agent User ka issue samajhta hai, relevant knowledge base search karta hai, ticket create karta hai agar zaroorat ho Travel Planning Agent Flights search karta hai, hotels compare karta hai, budget ke hisaab se recommend karta hai

docs.title: 11. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix No stopping condition/max iterations Agent infinite loop me phas sakta hai Always set max steps/timeout Giving agent too many tools without clear descriptions Agent confuse ho jata hai kaunsa tool kab use karna hai Clear, distinct tool descriptions do Not logging/tracing agent steps Debugging impossible ho jati hai jab kuch galat ho Use observability tools (LangSmith, etc.) to trace every step Using an agent when a simple chain would do Unnecessary complexity, cost, and unpredictability Use agents only when dynamic decision-making is truly needed No error handling for failed tool calls Agent crashes or gives bad output Build retry logic and graceful fallback responses

docs.title: One-Line Memory Tricks
docs.text:
• Chain → "Fixed route, developer ne decide kiya"
  • Agent → "Dynamic route, LLM khud decide karta hai"
  • ReAct → "Socho → Action lo → Dekho → Phir socho"
  • Planning → "Bade kaam ko chhote steps me todo"

docs.title: Quick Recap Flow
docs.text:
Goal Given → Agent Reasons (Thought) → Takes Action (Tool Call) 
→ Observes Result → Reasons Again → ... → Final Answer

docs.title: Golden Rule
docs.text: "Use a Chain when the path is known. Use an Agent when the LLM needs to figure out the path itself."

docs.title: API Design & Cost Optimization for LLM Apps — Complete Notes
docs.text: Yeh notes cover karte hain ki production-grade LLM applications kaise design ki jati hain — streaming, rate limiting, caching — aur cost ko kaise control/optimize kiya jata hai, jo AI Engineer ka ek daily concern hota hai.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Why This Matters
  2. Streaming Responses
  3. Rate Limiting
  4. Caching Strategies
  5. Prompt Caching (Special Case)
  6. Token Usage Optimization
  7. Model Selection Strategy (Cost vs Quality)
  8. Batching Requests
  9. Fallback & Retry Strategies
  10. Monitoring Cost in Production
  11. Common Mistakes
  12. Cheat Sheet

docs.title: 1. Why This Matters
docs.text:
LLM APIs traditional APIs se different hain kyunki: - Response turant nahi aata (LLM generation me time lagta hai — seconds tak) - Cost per-token based hota hai (traditional APIs usually free ya flat-rate hote hain) - High traffic me, rate limits aur cost explosion ka risk zyada hota hai

Isliye AI Engineer ko sirf "LLM se accha answer kaise le" nahi, balki "is answer ko efficiently, affordably, aur reliably user tak kaise pahunchayein" bhi sochna padta hai.

docs.title: 2. Streaming Responses
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Poore response ka wait karne ke bajaye, LLM ka output token-by-token (ya chunk-by-chunk) turant user ko dikhana shuru kar dena — jaise ChatGPT/Claude ki UI me text "type" hote hue dikhta hai.

docs.title: Why It's Important
docs.text:
• Perceived Speed: User ko lagta hai response fast aa raha hai, chahe total generation time same ho.
  • Better UX: Lambe responses ke liye, poora paragraph ek saath wait karne se better hai ki text gradually aaye.

docs.title: How It Works (Conceptual)
docs.text:
# Without streaming — user waits for the ENTIRE response
response = llm.generate(prompt)  # Blocks until fully complete
print(response)

# With streaming — tokens arrive incrementally
for chunk in llm.generate_stream(prompt):
    print(chunk, end="", flush=True)  # Display as it arrives

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• ✅ Chatbots, conversational UIs (almost always should stream)
  • ✅ Long-form content generation (articles, reports)
  • ⚪ Not necessary for backend/programmatic use where you just need the final JSON result

docs.title: 3. Rate Limiting
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Ek time period me, kitni requests ek user/system LLM API ko bhej sakta hai, uski limit set karna — taaki system overload na ho aur cost control me rahe.

docs.title: Why It's Needed
docs.text:
• LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI) khud bhi rate limits enforce karte hain (requests per minute, tokens per minute).
  • Aapke apne application me bhi rate limiting zaroori hai — taaki ek single user/bot poora system resources hijack na kar le, aur costs predictable rahein.

docs.title: Common Rate Limiting Strategies
docs.text: Strategy How It Works Fixed Window Ek fixed time window (e.g., "100 requests per minute") — window khatam hote hi reset Sliding Window Rolling time window — zyada smooth/fair distribution Token Bucket Har request ek "token" consume karta hai; tokens ek fixed rate se refill hote hain Per-User Limits Har user/API key ka apna alag limit Priority Queuing Important/paid users ko higher priority milti hai during high load

docs.title: Handling Rate Limit Errors
docs.text:
import time

def call_llm_with_retry(prompt, max_retries=3):
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            return llm.generate(prompt)
        except RateLimitError:
            wait_time = 2 ** attempt  # Exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s...
            time.sleep(wait_time)
    raise Exception("Max retries exceeded")

Exponential Backoff ek common pattern hai — har retry ke beech wait time double karte jao, taaki API pe pressure na bane.

docs.title: 4. Caching Strategies
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Agar same/similar request pehle bhi aa chuki hai, toh dobara LLM ko call karne ke bajaye, stored (cached) response wapas de do — isse cost aur latency dono bachte hain.

docs.title: Types of Caching
docs.text: Type How It Works Exact Match Caching Agar exact same prompt/query dobara aaye, cached response return karo Semantic Caching Agar similar meaning wala query aaye (exact match nahi, but semantically close), phir bhi cached response use karo

docs.title: Example — Exact Match Caching
docs.text:
cache = {}

def get_llm_response(prompt):
    if prompt in cache:
        return cache[prompt]  # Return cached, no LLM call needed

    response = llm.generate(prompt)
    cache[prompt] = response
    return response

docs.title: Example — Semantic Caching (Conceptual)
docs.text:
def get_llm_response_semantic(prompt):
    prompt_embedding = embed(prompt)

    # Search cache for a similar previous query (using vector similarity)
    similar_cached = search_cache_by_similarity(prompt_embedding, threshold=0.95)

    if similar_cached:
        return similar_cached.response  # Reuse cached answer

    response = llm.generate(prompt)
    save_to_cache(prompt_embedding, response)
    return response

docs.title: When Caching Helps Most
docs.text:
• FAQ-style bots (common repeated questions)
  • High-traffic applications with overlapping user queries
  • Static/rarely-changing information

docs.title: When Caching is Risky
docs.text:
• Personalized responses (different per user — caching could leak wrong info to wrong user)
  • Time-sensitive information (weather, stock prices — cached response could be stale/wrong)

docs.title: 5. Prompt Caching (Special Case)
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Modern LLM APIs (including Anthropic's) support caching parts of your prompt (especially long, repeated context like system prompts or large documents), so you don't pay full price to reprocess that same content on every request.

docs.title: How It Works (Conceptual)
docs.text:
Request 1: [Long System Prompt + Document Context] + "Question 1"
   → Full context processed, marked for caching

Request 2 (same session/context): [SAME Long System Prompt + Document Context] + "Question 2"
   → Cached portion reused at a MUCH lower cost — only "Question 2" is processed fresh

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• RAG systems jinme same large document context baar-baar use hota hai (multi-turn conversations over the same document), prompt caching dramatically cost kam kar sakta hai.
  • Especially useful for agents that repeatedly send the same tool definitions/system instructions in every turn.

docs.title: 6. Token Usage Optimization
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Prompt aur response me kam tokens use karna, bina quality kharab kiye — directly cost kam karta hai (kyunki billing per-token hoti hai).

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: Technique How It Helps Concise System Prompts Unnecessarily lambe instructions avoid karo Limit Retrieved Context Sirf top-K most relevant chunks bhejo (reranking se help milti hai — pichli notes) Truncate Long Conversations Sliding window / summarization memory use karo (pichli Memory notes) Set max_tokens appropriately Response length ko explicitly limit karo jab lamba answer zaroori na ho Use smaller models for simple tasks Har task ke liye sabse bada/expensive model zaroori nahi (next section)

docs.title: 7. Model Selection Strategy (Cost vs Quality)
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Har task ke liye sabse powerful (aur expensive) model use karna zaroori nahi — task ki complexity ke hisaab se right-sized model choose karo.

docs.title: Example Strategy
docs.text:
Simple Classification/Extraction Tasks → Smaller/Cheaper model (e.g., Haiku-tier)
Standard Q&A/Summarization → Mid-tier model (e.g., Sonnet-tier)
Complex Reasoning/Critical Decisions → Larger/Premium model (e.g., Opus-tier)

docs.title: Model Routing (Advanced)
docs.text:
• Ek router (chhota classifier ya rule-based logic) decide karta hai ki incoming request ki complexity kya hai, aur uske hisaab se appropriate model ko route karta hai.
Simple query → Cheap/Fast model
Complex query → Powerful/Expensive model

docs.title: - Yeh significantly cost bacha sakta hai bade scale pe, bina quality compromise kiye critical tasks pe.
8. Batching Requests
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Multiple independent requests ko ek saath (batch me) process karna, individually ek-ek karke bhejne ke bajaye.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Kuch providers batch APIs offer karte hain jo lower cost per request dete hain (trade-off: results turant nahi milte, thoda delay ke saath aate hain — asynchronous processing).
  • Useful for non-real-time tasks — jaise "saari overnight processing karo 10,000 documents ki, result kal subah tak chahiye."

docs.title: When to Use Batching
docs.text:
• ✅ Bulk data processing (classification, summarization of many documents)
  • ✅ Non-urgent, offline analysis tasks
  • ❌ Real-time chatbot responses (user turant jawab chahta hai)

docs.title: 9. Fallback & Retry Strategies
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Agar primary LLM call fail ho jaye (timeout, rate limit, server error), system ke paas ek backup plan hona chahiye.

docs.title: Common Strategies
docs.text: Strategy How It Works Retry with Backoff Thoda wait karke dobara try karo (exponential backoff) Fallback Model Agar primary model (jaise Opus) unavailable ho, ek secondary model (jaise Sonnet) use karo Fallback Response Agar sab kuch fail ho jaye, ek generic "Sorry, try again later" message do (crash hone se better) Circuit Breaker Pattern Agar ek service baar-baar fail ho raha hai, thodi der ke liye usko call karna hi band kar do (system ko overload hone se bachane ke liye), phir dobara try karo

docs.title: 10. Monitoring Cost in Production
docs.text:
(Yeh humari pichli Observability notes se directly connect hota hai)

What to Track Why Cost per request Understand unit economics of your application Cost per user/session Identify if certain usage patterns are disproportionately expensive Token usage trends over time Spot unexpected spikes (e.g., a bug causing huge prompts) Cost by model tier See if you're overusing expensive models where cheaper ones would suffice

docs.title: - Alert karo agar daily/monthly cost expected budget se significantly zyada ho jaye — taaki bugs (jaise infinite agent loops — pichli Agent notes yaad karo!) jaldi pakde jayein before they cause a huge bill.
11. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix Not streaming for user-facing chat apps Poor perceived performance, users think app is slow Implement streaming for all conversational interfaces No rate limiting on your own API Single user/bot could overwhelm system and spike costs Implement per-user rate limits No caching for repeated/common queries Paying full LLM cost for identical requests repeatedly Implement exact-match or semantic caching Always using the most powerful (expensive) model Overpaying for tasks that a cheaper model could handle Use model routing based on task complexity No retry/fallback logic Users see errors when a transient issue occurs Implement retry with backoff + fallback models/responses Not monitoring cost trends Bill spikes go unnoticed until the invoice arrives Set up cost dashboards and alerts (via observability tools)

docs.title: One-Line Memory Tricks
docs.text:
• Streaming → "Token-by-token dikhao, poora wait mat karwao"
  • Rate Limiting → "Ek time me kitni requests allowed hain, control karo"
  • Caching → "Same/similar sawal dobara pooche toh LLM mat bulao"
  • Prompt Caching → "Bada, repeated context sasta reprocess karo"
  • Model Routing → "Chhota kaam, chhota model — bada kaam, bada model"

docs.title: Quick Recap Flow
docs.text:
Request Comes In
   → [Rate Limit Check]
   → [Cache Check — return if cached]
   → [Model Router — pick right-sized model]
   → [Stream Response to User]
   → [If Error: Retry with Backoff → Fallback if needed]
   → [Log to Observability Tool — track cost/latency]

docs.title: Golden Rule
docs.text: "A great LLM app isn't just about generating good answers — it's about doing so reliably, quickly, and affordably at scale. Streaming, caching, rate limiting, and smart model selection are what separate a prototype from a production system."

docs.title: Advanced RAG Architectures — Complete Notes
docs.text: Basic RAG ek fixed, one-shot pipeline hai (Retrieve → Generate). Advanced RAG architectures isme self-checking, correction, aur agentic decision-making add karte hain, taaki system zyada accurate aur reliable ban sake.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Recap: What is "Naive/Basic" RAG
  2. Limitations of Basic RAG
  3. Self-RAG
  4. Corrective RAG (CRAG)
  5. Agentic RAG
  6. Adaptive RAG
  7. Comparison of All Architectures
  8. When to Use Which Architecture
  9. Common Mistakes
  10. Cheat Sheet

docs.title: 1. Recap: What is "Naive/Basic" RAG
docs.text:
User Query → Retrieve Top-K Chunks → Stuff into Prompt → LLM Generates Answer
  • Ek fixed, linear pipeline — hamesha yehi steps, chahe retrieval accha ho ya bura.
  • Koi self-checking nahi — system khud verify nahi karta ki retrieved info actually useful thi ya nahi.

docs.title: 2. Limitations of Basic RAG
docs.text:
Limitation Problem No Quality Check Agar retrieval bekaar/irrelevant chunks laaye, system phir bhi unhi se answer generate karega No Fallback Agar koi relevant info hi nahi mili, system phir bhi "kuch na kuch" answer bana dega (hallucination risk) Single-Shot Ek hi retrieval attempt — agar galat query se search hua, doosra try nahi hota No Iterative Refinement Agar answer incomplete/wrong nikla, system usko improve nahi karta

Advanced RAG architectures inhi problems ko solve karte hain — self-reflection, correction, aur dynamic decision-making add karke.

docs.title: 3. Self-RAG
docs.text: Simple Meaning: RAG system khud apne retrieval aur generation ko critique/evaluate karta hai, aur decide karta hai ki: - Retrieval zaroori hai bhi ya nahi (kuch queries ke liye retrieval ki zaroorat hi nahi hoti) - Retrieved chunks actually relevant hain ya nahi - Generated answer retrieved context se supported hai ya nahi

docs.title: How It Works (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Query aati hai
2. Model decide karta hai: "Kya iske liye retrieval chahiye?"
   → Agar NAHI (e.g., "2+2 kitna hai?"): Directly answer generate karo, retrieval skip karo
   → Agar HAAN: Retrieval karo

3. Retrieval ke baad, model self-evaluate karta hai:
   "Kya yeh retrieved chunks actually relevant hain?"
   → Agar NAHI: Discard karo ya dobara retrieve karo
   → Agar HAAN: Aage badho

4. Answer generate karne ke baad, model phir se self-evaluate karta hai:
   "Kya yeh answer retrieved context se supported/grounded hai?"
   → Agar NAHI: Answer ko revise karo
   → Agar HAAN: Final answer ke roop me return karo

docs.title: Special Tokens (Concept)
docs.text:
Self-RAG papers me, model ko special "reflection tokens" generate karne ke liye train kiya jata hai, jaise: - [Retrieve] / [No Retrieve] — retrieval chahiye ya nahi - [Relevant] / [Irrelevant] — retrieved chunk relevant hai ya nahi - [Supported] / [Not Supported] — answer context se grounded hai ya nahi

Yeh tokens model ke apne output ke andar generate hote hain, jo phir logic control karte hain (jaise agent ka conditional routing).

docs.title: Pros & Cons
docs.text:
• ✅ Unnecessary retrieval avoid karta hai (efficiency)
  • ✅ Bad/irrelevant retrievals ko catch karke correct karta hai
  • ✅ Hallucination kam karta hai (self-verification ki wajah se)
  • ❌ Extra reasoning steps → zyada latency/cost
  • ❌ Implementation complexity zyada hai basic RAG se

docs.title: 4. Corrective RAG (CRAG)
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Retrieval ke turant baad, ek lightweight evaluator (chhota classifier ya LLM check) retrieved chunks ki quality assess karta hai, aur uske hisaab se alag correction strategy apply karta hai.

docs.title: How It Works (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Query → Retrieve chunks (normal retrieval)
2. Evaluator checks retrieved chunks quality → Categorizes as:

   a) CORRECT (chunks are good/relevant)
      → Proceed normally with these chunks

   b) INCORRECT (chunks are irrelevant/bad)
      → Discard these chunks
      → Fall back to alternative source (e.g., web search) for better info

   c) AMBIGUOUS (partially relevant, unsure)
      → Combine retrieved chunks WITH additional web search results
      → Use both together for generation

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Query: "What are the latest features in React 19?"

Retrieved Chunks: [Old documentation about React 16 from internal knowledge base]

Evaluator: "These chunks are INCORRECT — they're about an older 
version and don't answer the 'latest' features question."

Correction Action: Trigger a web search for "React 19 new features" 
instead of relying on the outdated internal chunks.

Final Generation: Uses fresh web search results, not the stale internal docs.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: • Internal knowledge bases/vector stores ko regularly update karna difficult hota hai — CRAG isko compensate karta hai by falling back to live web search jab internal data insufficient/outdated lage.

docs.title: Pros & Cons
docs.text:
• ✅ Handles outdated/insufficient internal knowledge gracefully
  • ✅ Reduces risk of answering from bad/irrelevant retrieved context
  • ❌ Requires an additional evaluator component + possibly a web search integration
  • ❌ Adds latency (evaluation step + potential fallback search)

docs.title: 5. Agentic RAG
docs.text: Simple Meaning: RAG process ko ek agent ki tarah design karna — jahan agent dynamically decide karta hai kaunse retrieval sources use karne hain, kitni baar retrieve karna hai, aur kab "enough info" mil chuki hai.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Agent receives query
   │
   ▼
Agent reasons: "What information do I need, and where should I look?"
   │
   ▼
Agent may choose from MULTIPLE tools/sources:
   - Internal vector database
   - Web search
   - SQL database query
   - API calls
   │
   ▼
Agent retrieves from chosen source(s)
   │
   ▼
Agent reasons: "Do I have enough info now, or do I need to search more/differently?"
   │
   ▼ (Loop back if more info needed)
   │
   ▼
Agent generates final answer once satisfied

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Query: "Compare our Q3 sales performance to industry benchmarks."

Agentic RAG Process:
1. Agent decides: "I need our internal Q3 sales data" 
   → Queries internal SQL database
2. Agent decides: "I also need industry benchmark data"
   → Performs a web search for industry reports
3. Agent reasons: "I have both pieces of info now, I can compare them"
   → Generates comparative analysis using both sources

docs.title: Key Difference from Basic RAG
docs.text:
• Basic RAG: Ek fixed retrieval source, ek shot retrieval.
  • Agentic RAG: Multiple possible sources, dynamic multi-step retrieval, agent decides the strategy itself.

docs.title: Pros & Cons
docs.text:
• ✅ Bahut flexible — complex, multi-source information needs handle kar sakta hai
  • ✅ Multiple data sources ko intelligently combine kar sakta hai
  • ❌ Sabse zyada complex aur expensive (multiple LLM calls, multiple tool calls)
  • ❌ Debugging/predictability sabse difficult (agent unpredictable paths le sakta hai)

docs.title: 6. Adaptive RAG
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Query ki complexity ke hisaab se, system decide karta hai ki kaunsi RAG strategy use karni hai — simple query ke liye simple approach, complex query ke liye advanced/multi-step approach.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Query aati hai
   │
   ▼
Classifier/Router decides query complexity:

   - SIMPLE query (e.g., "What is the capital of France?")
     → No retrieval needed, or single simple retrieval

   - MODERATE query (needs specific document lookup)
     → Standard single-step RAG

   - COMPLEX query (multi-part, needs reasoning across sources)
     → Agentic RAG / Multi-step retrieval process

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• Efficiency: Har query ke liye same heavy process use karna wasteful hai — simple queries ko simple treatment do, complex ko complex treatment.
  • Cost aur latency ko query complexity ke hisaab se optimize karta hai.

docs.title: 7. Comparison of All Architectures
docs.text: Architecture Core Idea Complexity Key Benefit Basic RAG Fixed retrieve → generate ⭐ Low Simple, fast, cheap Self-RAG Model self-critiques retrieval & generation ⭐⭐⭐ High Reduces unnecessary retrieval + hallucination Corrective RAG (CRAG) Evaluates retrieval quality, falls back if bad ⭐⭐ Medium Handles outdated/bad internal data gracefully Agentic RAG Agent dynamically chooses sources/strategy ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Very High Handles complex, multi-source information needs Adaptive RAG Routes query to appropriate strategy based on complexity ⭐⭐⭐ High Optimizes cost/latency vs accuracy tradeoff

docs.title: 8. When to Use Which Architecture
docs.text:
Situation Recommended Simple Q&A over a stable, well-organized knowledge base Basic RAG Want to reduce hallucination and unnecessary retrieval Self-RAG Internal knowledge base might be outdated/incomplete Corrective RAG Need to pull from multiple different sources dynamically Agentic RAG Wide variety of query complexity (some simple, some very complex) Adaptive RAG Building an MVP/prototype quickly Basic RAG (upgrade later if needed)

Practical Advice: Start with Basic RAG. Only move to advanced architectures once you've measured (using the RAG evaluation metrics from earlier notes) that basic RAG has specific, identifiable weaknesses that these advanced patterns would solve.

docs.title: 9. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix Jumping straight to Agentic RAG for simple use cases Unnecessary complexity, cost, and latency Start simple, add complexity only when justified by measured need Not evaluating basic RAG's actual weaknesses first Building complex fixes for problems that may not exist Measure with retrieval/generation metrics before choosing an advanced architecture No fallback mechanism in production RAG System breaks/hallucinates when retrieval clearly fails Implement at least basic Corrective RAG-style fallback logic Ignoring cost implications of self-critiquing/multi-step approaches Bills can be significantly higher than basic RAG Monitor cost per query, weigh against accuracy gains

docs.title: One-Line Memory Tricks
docs.text:
• Self-RAG → "Khud apna kaam check karo — retrieval zaroori hai kya, sahi hai kya, answer grounded hai kya"
  • Corrective RAG → "Retrieval bekaar nikli toh fallback (web search) pe jao"
  • Agentic RAG → "Agent khud decide kare kahan se aur kitni baar retrieve karna hai"
  • Adaptive RAG → "Query ki complexity dekh ke strategy choose karo"

docs.title: Quick Decision Guide
docs.text:
Simple, stable knowledge base → Basic RAG
Need to reduce hallucination → Self-RAG
Internal data might be outdated → Corrective RAG
Multiple dynamic sources needed → Agentic RAG
Mixed complexity queries → Adaptive RAG

docs.title: Golden Rule
docs.text: "Advanced RAG architectures add self-awareness and correction to a pipeline that's otherwise 'blind' — but each layer of intelligence adds cost and complexity, so use only what your accuracy needs actually justify."

docs.title: Core AI Engineering Concepts — Complete Guide
docs.text: A foundational guide to the key concepts every AI Engineer must understand — tokens, context windows, RAG, embeddings, chunking, vector databases, prompting, agents, evaluation, and more.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Tokens
  2. Context Window
  3. Why RAG Exists
  4. Embeddings
  5. Real-World RAG Flow
  6. Chunking
  7. Chunking Strategies (Advanced)
  8. Vector Databases
  9. Similarity Search Algorithms
  10. Top-K Retrieval
  11. Relevance Filtering / Reranking
  12. Prompt Engineering
  13. System, User & Assistant Roles
  14. Temperature, Top-P & Sampling
  15. Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompt Engineering

docs.title: 1. Tokens
docs.text:
An LLM does not process words — it processes tokens. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, or even punctuation.

Example:

Input Token Split I love Flutter Splits into 3–4 tokens ProfilerLife Appointment Booking System Splits into multiple tokens

The more tokens involved: - The higher the cost (models charge per token — input + output) - The longer the processing time - The more context is consumed

Extra detail: Roughly, 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of a word in English. Different tokenizers (e.g., tiktoken for OpenAI models) split text differently, so token count varies model to model.

This is why understanding token management is essential for every AI Engineer.

docs.title: 2. Context Window
docs.text:
Suppose a model's context window is 128k tokens.

If you feed it: - 1 PDF - 100 chat messages - 20 pages of instructions

...all of this combined consumes the context window.

Once the context is full: - Older information may get dropped (truncated) - Response quality can degrade - In multi-turn chats, this is why long conversations start to "forget" earlier messages

This exact problem is what RAG is designed to solve.

Note: A bigger context window doesn't always mean better answers — models can suffer from the "lost in the middle" problem, where information placed in the middle of a very long context gets less attention than information at the start or end.

docs.title: 3. Why RAG Exists
docs.text:
Suppose you're building an AI chatbot that answers questions about ProfilerLife's documentation.

❌ Wrong Approach

Paste the entire documentation into the prompt.

Problems: - Expensive - Slow - Hits context limits

✅ Better Approach

User Question
     ↓
Search Relevant Docs
     ↓
Send Only Relevant Content to the Model
     ↓
Generate Answer

This is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) — the approach powering most chatbots and AI assistants in the industry today.

docs.title: 4. Embeddings
docs.text:
Now for one of the most important concepts.

A computer doesn't inherently understand that: - car - automobile - vehicle

...all carry the same meaning.

Embeddings solve this problem.

Embedding = converting text into numbers (a vector) that captures its meaning.

Example (simplified):

Word Vector car [0.82, 0.15, 0.91] vehicle [0.80, 0.17, 0.89] apple [0.05, 0.93, 0.12]

Notice: - The vectors for car and vehicle are similar. - The vector for apple is quite different.

This is what allows a system to perform semantic search.

Example: A user searches for "car insurance", and the database contains "vehicle coverage" — a match can still be found. This is the magic of embeddings.

How similarity is measured: once text is turned into vectors, we need a way to compare them — this is done using cosine similarity (measures the angle between two vectors) or sometimes dot product / Euclidean distance. Real embedding models (e.g., OpenAI text-embedding-3, Google text-embedding-004, open-source BGE, E5) produce vectors with hundreds or thousands of dimensions, not just 3.

docs.title: 5. Real-World RAG Flow
docs.text:
PDF Documents
     ↓
Chunking
     ↓
Embeddings
     ↓
Vector Database
     ↓
User Question
     ↓
Question Embedding
     ↓
Similarity Search
     ↓
Relevant Chunks
     ↓
LLM
     ↓
Final Answer

Every AI Engineer should have a solid understanding of this flow.

docs.title: 6. Chunking
docs.text:
Suppose you have a 100-page PDF.

If you generate a single embedding for the entire PDF: - Search accuracy suffers - Finding relevant information becomes difficult

To solve this, the document is split into smaller pieces called chunks.

Example:

Pages Chunk Page 1–3 Chunk A Page 4–6 Chunk B Page 7–9 Chunk C

Each chunk then gets its own embedding.

When a user asks:

"How does the provider claim flow work?"

The system doesn't process the entire PDF — it retrieves only the relevant chunks.

docs.title: 7. Chunking Strategies (Advanced)
docs.text:
How you chunk a document has a big impact on retrieval quality. Common strategies:

Strategy How it works Best for Fixed-size chunking Split every N tokens/characters Simple text, quick prototypes Overlapping chunks Each chunk shares some tokens with the next (e.g., 500 tokens, 50 overlap) Prevents cutting a sentence/idea in half Sentence/paragraph-based Split at natural sentence or paragraph boundaries Preserves meaning better Semantic chunking Split based on where the meaning shifts (using embeddings) High-accuracy RAG systems Recursive chunking Try splitting by paragraph first, then sentence, then character, as needed Long, structurally varied documents

Key tradeoff: - Too small chunks → lose context, answers feel incomplete - Too large chunks → dilute relevance, waste tokens, hurt retrieval precision

docs.title: 8. Vector Databases
docs.text:
Once chunks are converted into embeddings, they need to be stored somewhere that supports fast similarity search across millions of vectors. This is a vector database.

Vector DB Type Notes Pinecone Managed cloud Popular, easy to scale Chroma Open-source, local Great for prototypes FAISS (Meta) Library, not a full DB Extremely fast, in-memory Weaviate Open-source/cloud Supports hybrid search Qdrant Open-source/cloud Rust-based, high performance pgvector PostgreSQL extension Good if already using Postgres

A vector DB stores: - The embedding vector - The original text (or a reference to it) - Metadata (source, page number, date, tags — used for filtering)

docs.title: 9. Similarity Search Algorithms
docs.text:
Searching millions of vectors one-by-one (brute force) is too slow. Vector DBs use Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms to make this fast:

Algorithm Idea HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) Builds a graph structure for fast approximate search — most widely used IVF (Inverted File Index) Groups vectors into clusters, searches only relevant clusters LSH (Locality Sensitive Hashing) Hashes similar vectors into the same "bucket"

These trade a small amount of accuracy for a huge gain in speed — essential when working with millions/billions of vectors.

docs.title: 10. Top-K Retrieval
docs.text:
Real RAG systems typically use a setting like:

top_k = 3

This means if Top-K = 3, the system retrieves the 3 most similar chunks to the user's question, for example:

  1. Doc 3
  2. Doc 1
  3. Doc 2

Higher top_k → more context, but more tokens/cost and possible noise. Lower top_k → cheaper/faster, but risk of missing relevant info.

docs.title: 11. Relevance Filtering / Reranking
docs.text:
After retrieval, one more step often follows — reranking.

Document Relevance Doc 3 Very Relevant Doc 1 Somewhat Relevant Doc 2 Weak Relevance

Initial vector search (bi-encoder) is fast but approximate. A reranker (cross-encoder model, e.g., Cohere Rerank, BGE-reranker) re-scores the top candidates more precisely by looking at the query and each chunk together.

The system then sends only the best-ranked documents to the model for the final answer.

docs.title: 12. Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
The practice of designing inputs to get the best possible output from an LLM. Key techniques:

  • Be specific and clear — vague prompts give vague answers
  • Few-shot prompting — give 2–3 examples of input/output before the real task
  • Chain-of-thought — ask the model to "think step by step" for complex reasoning
  • Role prompting — "You are a senior Python developer..." sets behavior/tone
  • Output formatting — explicitly ask for JSON, markdown, bullet points, etc.
  • Negative examples — telling the model what not to do
Example (few-shot):

Classify sentiment as Positive/Negative/Neutral.

Text: "The food was amazing!" → Positive
Text: "It was okay, nothing special." → Neutral
Text: "Worst service ever." → Negative
Text: "I'll definitely come back again." → ?

docs.title: 13. System, User & Assistant Roles
docs.text:
Every conversation with an LLM is structured as a list of messages with roles:

Role Purpose system Sets the model's behavior, persona, and rules (usually invisible to the end user) user The actual question/input from the person assistant The model's response (also used to show prior turns for context) 
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful medical assistant. Never give a diagnosis."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "I have a headache, what should I do?"}
]

The system prompt is one of the most powerful tools in AI engineering — it controls tone, restrictions, and behavior across the whole conversation.

docs.title: 14. Temperature, Top-P & Sampling
docs.text:
These parameters control how random/creative the model's output is.

Parameter Effect temperature (0–2) Low (0–0.3) → focused, deterministic. High (0.7–1.5) → creative, varied top_p (nucleus sampling) Model only considers tokens whose cumulative probability adds up to p (e.g., 0.9) top_k (sampling) Model only considers the top k most likely next tokens max_tokens Limits the length of the generated response frequency/presence penalty Reduces repetition of words/phrases

⚠️ Don't confuse top_k (sampling) here with top_k (retrieval) from RAG — same name, completely different concept.

Rule of thumb: - Factual/coding tasks → low temperature (0–0.3) - Creative writing/brainstorming → higher temperature (0.7–1.0)

docs.title: 15. Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
Three different ways to make an LLM better at your specific task — often confused.

Approach What it does When to use Cost Prompt Engineering Just write better instructions Quick wins, simple tasks Free/cheapest RAG Feed relevant external knowledge at query time Need up-to-date or private/custom data Medium (embedding + storage cost) Fine-tuning Retrain the model on your own examples to change its behavior/style Need a consistent tone/format, or domain-specific behavior baked in Expensive, needs data + compute

Key insight: Fine-tuning teaches the model how to respond (style, format, behavior). RAG gives the model what to know (facts, current data). Most production systems use RAG, not fine-tuning, to keep knowledge updated.

docs.title: 16. Function Calling / Tool Use
docs.text:
LLMs can't browse the web, do math reliably, or access live data on their own — tool use (function calling) solves this.

How it works: 1. You describe available tools/functions to the model (name, parameters, description) 2. The model decides when a tool is needed and outputs a structured call (e.g., JSON) instead of plain text 3. Your code executes the actual function 4. The result is sent back to the model 5. The model uses that result to generate the final answer

{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "parameters": { "city": "Lahore" }
}

Real examples: searching the web, querying a database, calling a calculator, booking an appointment, sending an email.

docs.title: 17. AI Agents
docs.text:
An agent is an LLM that can reason, plan, and take actions using tools — in a loop — rather than just answering in one shot.

Typical agent loop:

Observe (user request + context)
     ↓
Think (reason about what to do next)
     ↓
Act (call a tool/function)
     ↓
Observe (tool result)
     ↓
Repeat until task is done
     ↓
Final Answer

This is often called the ReAct pattern (Reason + Act). Agents can chain multiple tool calls together to complete complex, multi-step tasks (e.g., "find flights, compare prices, and book the cheapest one").

docs.title: 18. Memory in AI Systems
docs.text:
LLMs are stateless by default — they don't remember past conversations unless you explicitly provide that history. AI systems handle memory in a few ways:

Type Description Short-term memory The current conversation's message history, resent every request Long-term memory Persisted facts/preferences about the user stored in a database and retrieved when relevant Episodic memory Summaries of past conversations/sessions Vector memory Past interactions stored as embeddings, retrieved via similarity search (similar to RAG)

Since context windows are limited, long conversations often get summarized periodically to save space while keeping important details.

docs.title: 19. Hallucinations
docs.text:
When a model generates information that sounds confident but is factually wrong or made up.

Why it happens: - The model is predicting the most likely next token, not verifying truth - No access to real-time/private data unless given via RAG or tools - Ambiguous or misleading prompts

How to reduce it: - Use RAG to ground answers in real documents - Lower temperature for factual tasks - Ask the model to cite sources/say "I don't know" when unsure - Add verification/fact-checking steps (another LLM call or human review)

docs.title: 20. Guardrails & Safety
docs.text:
Techniques used to keep AI systems safe, on-topic, and aligned with intended use:

  • Input validation — filtering harmful/irrelevant user input before it reaches the model
  • Output filtering — checking the model's response before showing it to the user (e.g., blocking PII leaks, toxic content)
  • System prompt restrictions — explicitly telling the model what it must not do
  • Rate limiting — preventing abuse/prompt injection attacks
  • Prompt injection defense — ensuring untrusted content (e.g., a scraped webpage) can't hijack the model's instructions

docs.title: 21. Evaluation Metrics
docs.text:
How AI engineers measure if a system (especially RAG/LLM apps) is actually performing well:

Metric Measures Retrieval Precision/Recall Did we retrieve the right chunks? Faithfulness Does the answer stay true to the retrieved context (no hallucination)? Relevance Is the final answer actually relevant to the question? Latency How long does the response take? BLEU / ROUGE Compare generated text to a reference text (common in summarization/translation) Human evaluation Manual review — still the gold standard for subjective quality

docs.title: 22. Streaming Responses
docs.text:
Instead of waiting for the entire response to be generated, the model can stream tokens one-by-one as they're produced — this is why ChatGPT-style apps show text appearing word-by-word.

Benefits: - Better perceived speed/UX - User can start reading before generation finishes - Can be stopped early if needed (saves cost)

for chunk in response_stream:
    print(chunk.text, end="")

docs.title: 23. Latency & Cost Optimization
docs.text:
Practical techniques AI engineers use in production:

  • Caching — store responses to repeated/common queries (e.g., lru_cache, Redis)
  • Smaller/faster models for simple tasks, larger models only when needed (model routing)
  • Batching requests where possible
  • Reducing token usage — shorter prompts, smaller top_k, better chunking
  • Prompt caching — reusing a static portion of a prompt (e.g., system prompt) to avoid reprocessing it every call
  • Async/parallel calls for independent tasks (e.g., multiple tool calls at once)

docs.title: 24. Quantization
docs.text:
A technique to make models smaller and faster by reducing the precision of their internal numbers (weights).

Precision Size Speed Quality FP32 (full) Largest Slowest Highest FP16 / BF16 Half Faster Very close to FP32 INT8 Quarter Much faster Slight quality drop INT4 Even smaller Fastest Noticeable quality drop (task-dependent)

Why it matters: quantization lets large models run on smaller/cheaper hardware (even laptops/phones) with a manageable tradeoff in accuracy.

docs.title: 25. Multi-Modal Models
docs.text:
Models that can understand/generate more than just text:

Modality Example Text + Image Describe an image, answer questions about a chart/photo Text + Audio Speech-to-text, voice assistants Text + Video Summarize/analyze video content Text-to-Image Generate images from text prompts

Multi-modal embeddings work the same way as text embeddings — different data types are converted into vectors that live in a shared "meaning space," enabling cross-modal search (e.g., searching images using a text query).

docs.title: 26. Popular Frameworks
docs.text:
Tools that make building RAG pipelines and agents faster (instead of writing everything from scratch):

Framework Purpose LangChain Chains, RAG pipelines, agents, tool integrations LlamaIndex Focused heavily on data indexing/retrieval for RAG Haystack Production-grade RAG/search pipelines CrewAI / AutoGen Multi-agent orchestration frameworks LangGraph Building stateful, graph-based agent workflows

docs.title: 27. Model Context Protocol (MCP)
docs.text:
A standardized protocol (introduced by Anthropic) that lets AI models connect to external tools, data sources, and apps in a consistent way — instead of every app building its own custom integration.

Why it matters: it allows an LLM-based assistant to plug into things like file systems, databases, or third-party apps (calendars, project trackers, etc.) through a common interface, making tool integrations more standardized and reusable across different AI applications.

docs.title: 28. Quick Summary Table
docs.text:
Concept One-line takeaway Tokens The real unit of cost/length for LLMs Context Window Limited "memory" per request RAG Retrieve relevant info instead of stuffing everything into the prompt Embeddings Turn text into meaning-preserving numbers Chunking Break large documents into searchable pieces Vector DB Stores embeddings for fast similarity search Top-K How many chunks to retrieve Reranking Re-score retrieved chunks for better precision Prompt Engineering Better instructions = better outputs Temperature/Top-P Controls randomness/creativity Fine-tuning Changes model behavior/style permanently Function Calling Lets the model use external tools Agents LLMs that reason + act in a loop Memory How systems remember past context Hallucination Confident but wrong output Guardrails Keep the system safe and on-topic Evaluation How you know the system actually works Quantization Smaller/faster models, small quality tradeoff Multi-modal Understanding text, images, audio, video together

Yeh guide RAG pipelines, AI engineering interviews, aur system design discussions ke liye ek complete conceptual foundation deta hai.

docs.title: AI Ethics & Bias
docs.text: Simple notes on why AI can behave unfairly or harmfully, and the key ethical concerns around it.

docs.title: 1. What is AI Bias?
docs.text:
Simple definition: AI Bias happens when an AI system gives unfair or skewed results for certain groups of people — usually because the data it learned from was biased, not because the AI is "intentionally" being unfair.

Remember: AI learns from data. If the data has bias, the AI will learn that bias too. "Garbage in, garbage out."

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A company builds an AI to shortlist job resumes by training it on 10 years of past hiring data. - If the company mostly hired men in the past (even if unintentionally), the AI learns that pattern - It starts favoring male candidates and rejecting equally qualified female candidates - This actually happened — Amazon scrapped an AI hiring tool in 2018 for exactly this reason

Other real examples: - Facial recognition systems being less accurate for darker-skinned faces (trained mostly on lighter-skinned faces) - Loan approval AI rejecting minority applicants more often, because historical loan data reflected past discrimination - Voice assistants understanding certain accents better than others

docs.title: 2. Where Does Bias Come From?
docs.text: Source Explanation Example Biased Training Data Data reflects real-world historical inequalities Hiring data with fewer women in tech roles Unbalanced Data Some groups are underrepresented in the dataset Facial recognition trained mostly on one skin tone Human Bias in Labeling Humans labeling data bring their own biases Labeling certain speech as "aggressive" based on accent/dialect Design Choices Developers unintentionally build assumptions into the system An app assuming everyone has a smartphone/internet

docs.title: a) Bias & Fairness
docs.text: AI should treat all groups of people fairly — covered above.

docs.title: b) Privacy
docs.text:
AI models are often trained on huge amounts of data — sometimes including personal or sensitive information without proper consent.

Example: An AI trained on social media posts might accidentally memorize and reveal someone's private details.

docs.title: c) Transparency (Explainability)
docs.text:
Many AI models are a "black box" — even the developers don't fully know why it gave a specific answer.

Example: A bank's AI rejects your loan application, but no one — not even the bank — can clearly explain why the AI decided that.

docs.title: d) Accountability
docs.text:
If an AI makes a harmful mistake, who is responsible — the company, the developer, or the AI itself?

Example: A self-driving car causes an accident. Is it the car manufacturer's fault, the software developer's fault, or the AI's "fault"?

docs.title: e) Misinformation & Deepfakes
docs.text:
AI can generate very convincing fake text, images, audio, or video — which can be used to spread false information or impersonate real people.

Example: A fake AI-generated video of a political leader saying something they never actually said.

docs.title: f) Job Displacement
docs.text:
AI automating tasks can replace human jobs, raising concerns about employment and economic impact.

Example: AI writing tools reducing the need for certain content-writing jobs.

docs.title: 4. How Companies Try to Reduce Bias & Improve Ethics
docs.text: Method What It Does Diverse Training Data Include data representing many groups, backgrounds, accents, skin tones, etc. Bias Testing/Auditing Regularly test the AI's outputs across different groups to catch unfair patterns Human Review Keep humans in the loop for important decisions (hiring, loans, medical) instead of fully automating them Transparency Reports Companies publishing how their models are trained and tested Guardrails/Safety Training Fine-tuning models (like RLHF) to refuse harmful requests and reduce toxic/biased outputs

docs.title: 5. Simple Analogy
docs.text:
Think of AI like a student who only studied from one textbook written by one biased author:

  • If that textbook mostly talked about one group of people, ignored others, or had unfair stereotypes...
  • The student (AI) will repeat those same biases and gaps when answering questions — not because the student is "evil," but because that's all it was taught.

The fix: give the student better, more diverse, and fact-checked textbooks (better training data) — and teach them to question and double-check their assumptions (bias auditing + human review).

docs.title: 6. Key Terms (Quick Glossary)
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning Bias Unfair favoritism or discrimination in AI outputs Fairness Ensuring AI treats all groups equitably Black Box Model An AI system whose internal decision-making isn't easily explainable Explainability/Interpretability Being able to understand why an AI made a certain decision Deepfake AI-generated fake image/video/audio that looks/sounds real Guardrails Built-in rules/training that stop an AI from generating harmful or biased content Human-in-the-loop Keeping a human involved in reviewing/approving AI decisions, especially for important matters

docs.title: One-Line Summary (for quick revision)
docs.text:
• AI Bias → Unfair outputs caused by biased or unbalanced training data ("garbage in, garbage out").
  • Ethics concerns → Bias/fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability, misinformation, job impact.
  • Fix approach → Diverse data + bias testing + human review + transparency + safety fine-tuning.
  • Analogy → AI is like a student who only learned from one biased textbook — better textbooks (data) = better student (AI).

docs.title: Hallucination in AI — Deep Dive
docs.text: Simple notes on why AI sometimes confidently gives wrong or made-up answers.

docs.title: 1. What is AI Hallucination?
docs.text:
Simple definition: Hallucination happens when an AI model confidently generates information that is false, made-up, or doesn't actually exist — but presents it as if it were true.

  • It's not "lying" on purpose — the model has no concept of true vs false, it just predicts the most statistically likely next word
  • It happens with text, but also with images, citations, code, facts, dates, quotes — anything the model generates

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
You ask: "Who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2025 for research on XYZ?"

If the model doesn't actually know or wasn't trained on that specific fact, it might still generate a confident-sounding, completely made-up name — because it's designed to always produce a plausible-sounding response, not to say "I don't know" by default.

Other real examples: - A lawyer used ChatGPT for legal research, and it cited fake court cases that don't exist — this actually happened and caused real legal trouble - Asking an AI for a book's exact quote → it may generate a quote that sounds right but was never actually written - Asking for a citation/source → it may invent a realistic-looking but fake URL or paper title

docs.title: 2. Why Does Hallucination Happen?
docs.text: Reason Explanation Predicts "likely" words, not "true" facts The model is fundamentally a next-word predictor — it generates whatever sounds most probable/fluent, not necessarily what's factually verified No built-in fact-checking Unless connected to search/tools, the model can't verify its answer against real-world facts in real time Gaps in training data If the model wasn't trained on specific/rare information, it may "fill in the blank" with something plausible-sounding instead of admitting it doesn't know Ambiguous or leading prompts Vague questions or questions that assume something false can push the model to "go along" with a false premise Overconfidence in generation style Models are trained to sound fluent and confident — which can make wrong answers sound just as convincing as correct ones

docs.title: 3. Simple Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine asking a very well-read friend a question they don't actually know the answer to — but instead of saying "I'm not sure," they confidently make up something that sounds believable, based on similar things they've heard before.

  • They're not trying to deceive you
  • They just have a strong instinct to always give you a smooth, confident-sounding answer — even when they should really just say "I don't know"

That's exactly what an AI hallucination is: confident, fluent, but factually wrong.

docs.title: 4. Types of Hallucination
docs.text: Type Example Factual Hallucination Giving a wrong date, name, or statistic as if it's correct Fabricated Sources Inventing fake citations, links, book titles, or research papers Logical Hallucination Making a reasoning error that sounds logical but isn't actually correct Instruction Hallucination Claiming to have done something (like "I've searched the web") when it actually hasn't, unless tools are properly used

docs.title: 5. How to Reduce Hallucination (What Helps)
docs.text: Method How It Helps RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) Model looks up real info before answering, instead of relying on memory (covered in your earlier notes) Web Search / Tool Use Letting the model search the internet or a database for current, verified facts Asking for sources & double-checking Always verify important facts, citations, or numbers independently Being specific in your prompt Clear, specific questions reduce the model's need to "guess"/fill gaps Lower "creativity" settings (temperature) Reduces randomness, making the model stick closer to safer, more predictable answers Fine-tuning for honesty Training the model to say "I'm not sure" instead of guessing, when appropriate

docs.title: 6. What YOU Should Do As a User
docs.text:
✅ Always double-check: - Statistics, dates, and numbers - Legal, medical, or financial facts - Citations, quotes, and links - Anything critical for real decisions (exams, business, legal matters)

✅ Ask the AI to search the web (if the tool is available) for anything time-sensitive or fact-critical

✅ Treat AI like a smart but sometimes-wrong assistant — not an infallible source of truth

docs.title: 7. Key Terms (Quick Glossary)
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning Hallucination AI confidently generating false/made-up information Grounding Connecting AI answers to real, verified sources (e.g., via RAG or search) Temperature A setting controlling how "creative"/random vs "safe"/predictable the model's output is Confabulation Another term sometimes used for AI "making things up" confidently Fact-checking Verifying AI-generated claims against real, reliable sources

docs.title: Where This Fits
docs.text:
Generative AI generates text by predicting "likely" words
   → Sometimes "likely-sounding" ≠ "factually true"
        → This gap = Hallucination
             → Fixed/reduced using: RAG, Web Search, better prompting, human verification

docs.title: One-Line Summary (for quick revision)
docs.text:
• Hallucination → AI confidently generating false or made-up information, because it predicts "likely" text, not verified "true" facts.
  • Why it happens → No built-in fact-checking, gaps in training data, and a tendency to sound fluent/confident regardless of accuracy.
  • Fix → RAG, web search/tool use, specific prompts, and always double-checking critical facts yourself.
  • Analogy → Like a well-read friend who'd rather guess confidently than admit "I don't know."

docs.title: AI Model Deployment — Basics
docs.text: Simple notes on taking your AI model/app from "works on my laptop" to "live and usable by real people."

docs.title: 1. What is Deployment?
docs.text:
Simple definition: Deployment means making your AI app/model available and running on the internet (usually on a server/cloud), so real users (not just you, on your laptop) can actually use it.

Building a model = cooking a great dish in your home kitchen. Deployment = opening a restaurant so customers can actually order and eat that dish, anytime.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: You build a chatbot using Claude's API + FastAPI on your laptop. It works when you run it locally. - Not deployed: Only YOU can use it, only when your laptop is on and running the code - Deployed: It's running on a server 24/7, at a real URL (e.g., mychatbot.com), and anyone can use it, anytime

docs.title: 2. Why Deployment Is a Whole Skill (Not Just "Uploading Code")
docs.text: Challenge What It Means Availability Your app needs to run 24/7, not just when your laptop is open Scalability If 10,000 people use it at once, it shouldn't crash Consistency It should behave the same way for every user, every time (this is where Docker helps — from your last notes!) Security Protecting user data, API keys, and preventing abuse Monitoring Knowing if/when something breaks, and fixing it fast Cost management Cloud servers cost money — you don't want to overpay for resources you're not using

docs.title: 3. The Basic Deployment Pipeline (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Build the app        →  Your AI logic + FastAPI (from last notes)
2. Package it            →  Put it in a Docker container (consistent everywhere)
3. Choose a hosting place →  A cloud provider (AWS, GCP, Azure, Render, Railway, etc.)
4. Deploy it              →  Upload/run the container on that server
5. Get a live URL          →  e.g., https://myapp.com
6. Monitor & maintain      →  Watch for errors, traffic, and update as needed

docs.title: Example (Full Flow, Tying Everything Together)
docs.text:
1. You build a FastAPI app that calls Claude's API to answer questions (from your FastAPI notes)
  2. You package it into a Docker container (from your Docker notes) — so it runs identically anywhere
  3. You choose a cloud platform (e.g., AWS or a simpler option like Render/Railway)
  4. You deploy the container there
  5. Now your chatbot is live at https://myaichatbot.com — real users can visit and chat with it
  6. You monitor it to make sure it stays up and handles traffic well

docs.title: 4. Where Can You Deploy? (Common Options)
docs.text: Option Simple Meaning Good For Cloud Providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) Big, powerful, flexible — you rent servers/services Large-scale, production apps PaaS (Platform as a Service) (Render, Railway, Heroku) Simplified deployment — less setup, more beginner-friendly Smaller projects, quick launches, learning Serverless (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions) You don't manage servers at all — code runs only when triggered, and you pay only for actual usage Occasional/light-traffic tasks, cost-saving Model Hosting Platforms (Hugging Face Spaces, Replicate) Specifically built for hosting AI/ML models easily Quick AI model demos/APIs

docs.title: 5. Simple Analogy (Full Restaurant Analogy)
docs.text: Concept Restaurant Analogy Your AI model/code The recipe & cooking skill FastAPI The waiter — takes orders (requests), delivers food (responses) Docker Standardized kitchen equipment/setup — same setup works in any restaurant location Cloud Server The actual restaurant building/location Deployment Opening the restaurant — now customers can actually walk in and order Scaling Opening more restaurant branches when demand grows Monitoring Restaurant manager watching for problems (long wait times, complaints, etc.)

docs.title: 6. Key Concepts You'll Hear in Deployment/MLOps
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning CI/CD (Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment) Automatically testing and deploying your app every time you update the code — no manual re-uploading Scaling Automatically running more copies of your app when there's more traffic, and fewer when there's less Load Balancer Distributes incoming user traffic across multiple copies of your app, so no single server gets overwhelmed Environment Variables Secret settings (like API keys) kept separate from your code, so they stay secure Monitoring/Logging Tools that track errors, performance, and usage so you know when something breaks MLOps The broader practice of deploying, monitoring, and maintaining AI/ML models in production (like "DevOps," but for ML) Latency How long it takes for your app to respond — important for a smooth user experience API Key A secret code that authorizes your app to use a service (e.g., Claude's API) — must be kept private

docs.title: 7. Common Beginner Mistakes in Deployment
docs.text: Mistake Why It's a Problem Fix Hardcoding API keys in code Security risk — anyone who sees your code can steal it Use environment variables/secrets instead Not testing before deploying Bugs go live and affect real users Test locally, then in a "staging" environment first No monitoring You won't know if the app crashes until users complain Set up basic logging/alerts Ignoring cost Cloud bills can grow fast if not managed Monitor usage, use free tiers for learning/small projects No scaling plan App crashes under sudden high traffic Use platforms with auto-scaling, even for small projects

docs.title: Where This Fits (Full AI Engineering Picture)
docs.text:
1. AI Model/Logic       →  The "brain" (e.g., Claude API call, or your own trained model)
2. FastAPI               →  Exposes it as a usable API ("waiter")
3. Docker                →  Packages it consistently ("standardized kitchen")
4. Cloud/Hosting         →  Where it actually runs ("restaurant location")
5. Deployment            →  Making it live for real users ("opening the restaurant")
6. MLOps/Monitoring      →  Keeping it running well over time ("restaurant management")

docs.text:
• Deployment → Making your AI app/model live on the internet so real users can actually use it, 24/7.
  • Pipeline → Build → Package (Docker) → Host (cloud) → Deploy → Monitor.
  • MLOps → The ongoing practice of deploying, scaling, and maintaining AI models in production.
  • Analogy → Deployment = opening your restaurant to real customers, after perfecting the recipe (model) and setting up the kitchen (Docker) and waiter (FastAPI).

docs.title: BM25 Algorithm — Notes
docs.text: BM25 (Best Matching 25) is a ranking algorithm used in search engines and RAG retrieval systems to score how relevant a document is to a given query. Yeh keyword-based (sparse) retrieval algorithm hai — matlab yeh exact word matching pe kaam karta hai (embeddings/meaning wale semantic search se alag).

docs.title: Simple Meaning
docs.text:
BM25 batata hai: "Yeh document is query ke liye kitna relevant hai?"

Isko score karne ke liye teen cheezein dekhta hai: 1. Query ke words document me kitni baar aaye (Term Frequency) 2. Woh word kitna rare/common hai poore corpus me (Inverse Document Frequency) 3. Document ki length — kaheen document sirf lamba hone ki wajah se zyada match toh nahi kar raha (Length Normalization)

docs.title: Why BM25? (Background)
docs.text:
• Purana simple method tha TF (Term Frequency) — jitni baar word aaya utna zyada score. Problem: common words (the, is, a) bhi high score paate the.
  • Fir aaya TF-IDF — rare words ko zyada importance di gayi.
  • BM25 TF-IDF ka hi improved/smarter version hai — yeh saturation (ek limit ke baad word repeat hone ka effect kam karna) aur document length normalization bhi handle karta hai.

docs.title: The Formula
docs.text:
N
BM25(D, Q) = Σ  IDF(qi) × [ f(qi, D) × (k1 + 1) ] / [ f(qi, D) + k1 × (1 - b + b × |D|/avgdl) ]
                   i=1

Yeh dekhne me complex lagta hai, par har part ko todke samjhte hain 👇

docs.title: 1. IDF(qi) — Inverse Document Frequency
docs.text:
Simple meaning: Yeh word kitna rare/special hai poore corpus (saare documents) me.

IDF(qi) = log( (N - n(qi) + 0.5) / (n(qi) + 0.5) + 1 )
  • N = total number of documents in the corpus
  • n(qi) = number of documents that contain the term qi

Intuition: - Agar word bahut common hai (jaise "the", "is") → low IDF (kam importance) - Agar word rare hai (jaise "photosynthesis") → high IDF (zyada importance)

Rare word mile toh matlab match "special" hai, common word mile toh koi badi baat nahi.

docs.title: 2. f(qi, D) — Term Frequency in Document
docs.text:
Simple meaning: Query ka word qi, document D me kitni baar aaya.

  • Jitni baar word repeat hua, utna zyada relevant maana jayega — but with a limit (saturation), isiliye neeche k1 aata hai.

docs.title: 3. k1 — Term Frequency Saturation Parameter
docs.text:
Simple meaning: Yeh control karta hai ki word repeat hone ka effect kitni jaldi saturate (flatten) ho jaye.

  • Typical value: k1 = 1.2 to 2.0
  • Agar word 1 baar aaya vs 20 baar aaya — bina saturation ke, 20 baar wale ka score bahut zyada high ho jayega (jo galat hai, kyunki keyword-stuffing possible hai).
  • BM25 isko control karta hai — after a point, extra repetitions ka score pe bahut kam effect padta hai.

Socho: Ek genuine article me keyword 3-4 baar aana natural hai, lekin 50 baar aana spam jaisa lagta hai — BM25 uss "diminishing returns" ko handle karta hai.

docs.title: 4. b — Length Normalization Parameter
docs.text:
Simple meaning: Yeh control karta hai ki document ki length kitna effect dalti hai score pe.

  • Typical value: b = 0.75
  • Range: 0 (no length normalization) to 1 (full length normalization)
|D|    = length of document D (number of words)
avgdl  = average document length across the whole corpus

Intuition: - Bina normalization ke, lambe documents naturally zyada word-matches paayenge (bas iss wajah se ki unme zyada text hai) — yeh unfair advantage hai. - b isko balance karta hai — chota document agar relevant hai toh usko bhi fair chance milta hai lambe document ke against.

docs.title: Putting It All Together — Full Intuition
docs.text:
For each query word:

Score = IDF(word) × [ (word repeats in doc) adjusted for saturation and doc length ]

Final document score = sum of scores for all query words.

docs.title: Worked Example (Simplified)
docs.text:
Query: "cat food"

Document A: "The cat loves cat food and cat toys" (word "cat" appears 3 times, document is short) Document B: "A very long article about pets, animals, dogs, cats, and various food items across many pages..." (word "cat" appears once, but document is very long)

Factor Document A Document B Term Frequency of "cat" High (3) Low (1) Document Length Short Very Long Effect Score is high, and not too long so no penalty Score is diluted — even though "cat" appeared, document length brings score down

Result: BM25 will likely rank Document A higher — it has good keyword frequency without being unnaturally long.

docs.title: BM25 vs TF-IDF vs Semantic Search (Embeddings)
docs.text:
Feature TF-IDF BM25 Semantic Search (Embeddings) Based on Exact word match Exact word match (smarter) Meaning/context (vectors) Handles synonyms? ❌ No ❌ No ✅ Yes Handles saturation (repeated words)? ❌ No ✅ Yes (via k1) N/A Handles document length bias? ❌ Weak ✅ Yes (via b) N/A Good for Simple keyword search Robust keyword-based search Understanding intent/meaning Common use today Legacy systems Hybrid RAG search (with vectors) Modern RAG search

Note: In modern RAG systems, BM25 is often combined with vector/embedding search — this is called Hybrid Search. BM25 catches exact keyword matches (e.g., product codes, names), while embeddings catch semantic/meaning-based matches.

docs.title: Key Parameters Summary
docs.text: Parameter Meaning Typical Value k1 Controls term frequency saturation 1.2 – 2.0 b Controls document length normalization 0.75 N Total documents in corpus Depends on dataset n(qi) Number of docs containing word qi Depends on dataset avgdl Average document length in corpus Depends on dataset

docs.title: Why BM25 Still Matters in RAG (2024-2026 era)
docs.text:
• Even with powerful embedding models, BM25 is still used because:
  • It's fast and cheap (no GPU needed).
  • It's great at exact matches — IDs, names, codes, rare technical terms that embeddings sometimes miss.
  • Combined with vector search in Hybrid RAG, it improves overall retrieval accuracy (Hit Rate, Recall, NDCG — the metrics from your previous notes!).

docs.title: One-Line Memory Trick
docs.text:
BM25 = "Kitni baar mila (TF) × Kitna rare hai (IDF) — lekin bahut zyada repeat aur bahut lamba document mat gin"

  • k1 → "Repeat hone ki himmat kam karo after a point"
  • b → "Lamba document hone ka fayda mat do"
  • IDF → "Rare word = zyada importance"

docs.title: Chunking in RAG — Complete Notes
docs.text: Chunking = Bade documents ko chhote-chhote pieces (chunks) me todna, taaki RAG system unhe efficiently store, search aur retrieve kar sake. Yeh RAG pipeline ka sabse important step hai — agar chunking galat hui, toh retrieval aur generation dono kharab honge, chahe embedding model kitna bhi accha ho.

docs.title: Why Chunking is Needed (Simple Reason)
docs.text:
1. LLMs ki context window limited hoti hai — pura document ek saath nahi de sakte.
  2. Embedding models bhi ek limit tak hi text ko accurately represent kar sakte hain — bahut lamba text dene se meaning "dilute" ho jata hai.
  3. Precise Retrieval — Chote, focused chunks se sirf relevant info milti hai, pura irrelevant document nahi.

Analogy: Socho ek poori kitab ko dhoondhne ke bajaye, sirf uska relevant paragraph nikal ke doctor/lawyer ko dena — zyada useful hai.

docs.title: Golden Rule of Chunking
docs.text: "Chunk chhota ho par complete meaning wala ho — na bahut chhota (context lost), na bahut bada (irrelevant info mix ho jaye)."

docs.title: Overview Table — All Chunking Types
docs.text: Type Based On Complexity Best For Fixed-Size Chunking Character/token count ⭐ Easy Simple, generic text Recursive Character Chunking Hierarchical separators (paragraph→sentence→word) ⭐⭐ Medium General purpose (most common default) Sentence-Based Chunking Sentence boundaries ⭐⭐ Medium Q&A, precise answers Semantic Chunking Meaning/similarity of text ⭐⭐⭐ Advanced High-accuracy RAG Document-Based/Structural Chunking Document structure (headings, sections) ⭐⭐ Medium Structured docs (manuals, legal, wiki) Sliding Window Chunking Overlapping fixed windows ⭐⭐ Medium Preserving context across boundaries Agentic / LLM-Based Chunking LLM decides chunk boundaries ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Advanced Complex, high-value documents Table/Code-Aware Chunking Special content type (tables, code) ⭐⭐⭐ Advanced Technical docs, code repos Parent-Child Chunking Two-level chunks (big + small) ⭐⭐⭐ Advanced Long structured docs needing context + precision Late Chunking Embed full doc first, split after ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Advanced Docs with heavy pronoun/reference usage, need context-aware embeddings

docs.title: 1. Fixed-Size Chunking
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Document ko ek fixed number of characters/tokens me todo — bas seedha count karke split karo.

docs.title: How it Works
docs.text:
• Choose a chunk size (e.g., 500 tokens or 1000 characters).
  • Cut the text every N tokens/characters, regardless of sentence or paragraph boundaries.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Chunk size = 100 characters

Chunk 1: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. Machine learning is a subs..."
Chunk 2: "et of artificial intelligence that focuses on..."

(Notice: word "subset" got cut in between — "subs" and "et" split across chunks!)

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Very simple and fast to implement.
  • ✅ Predictable chunk sizes (good for embedding models with token limits).

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• ❌ Can cut sentences/words in the middle, breaking meaning.
  • ❌ Doesn't respect any natural structure of the document.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text: • Quick prototypes, simple projects, or when document structure doesn't matter much.

docs.title: 2. Recursive Character/Text Chunking (Most Common Default)
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Pehle bade separators (paragraph) se todne ki koshish karo, agar chunk phir bhi bada hai, toh chhote separators (sentence, phir word) pe jao.

docs.title: How it Works
docs.text:
Hierarchy of separators, tried in order:

1. Try splitting by "\n\n" (paragraphs)
2. If still too big → split by "\n" (lines)
3. If still too big → split by ". " (sentences)
4. If still too big → split by " " (words)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• A long paragraph gets split at paragraph breaks first.
  • If a single paragraph is still too long, it further breaks it at sentence level.

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Respects natural document structure much better than fixed-size.
  • ✅ Balances chunk size with meaning preservation.
  • ✅ Most popular default method (used in LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter).

docs.title: Cons
docs.text: • ❌ Still can occasionally split mid-thought if paragraphs/sentences are very long.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text: • Default choice for most RAG projects — general-purpose documents (articles, blogs, reports).
