  • No labeled data, no fixed patterns to find
  • It learns by doing, through feedback (reward/punishment)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Teaching an AI to play a video game: - It tries random moves at first - Move helps win points → Reward (+1) → "do more of this" - Move causes it to lose/die → Penalty (-1) → "avoid this" - After thousands of attempts, it learns the best strategy to win

Other examples: - Self-driving cars learning to drive safely (reward: smooth safe driving, penalty: crash) - Robots learning to walk (reward: staying balanced, penalty: falling) - AI mastering games like Chess/Go (AlphaGo learned this way)

Think of it like: Training a dog with treats — good behavior gets a treat (reward), bad behavior doesn't, and over time the dog learns what to do.

docs.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text: Feature Supervised Unsupervised Reinforcement Data type Labeled (input + correct answer) Unlabeled (input only) No fixed data — learns via actions & feedback Human involvement High (labels answers) Low (no labels needed) Medium (defines rewards/penalties) Goal Predict correct output Find hidden patterns/groups Learn best action/strategy Example Spam detection Customer segmentation Game-playing AI, robots Analogy Studying with answer key Sorting items without labels Training a dog with treats

docs.title: Where This Fits
docs.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI)
   └── Machine Learning (ML)
          ├── Supervised Learning
          ├── Unsupervised Learning
          └── Reinforcement Learning
                 └── (Deep Learning can be used inside any of these three,
                      using Neural Networks as the underlying model)

docs.title: One-Line Summary (for quick revision)
docs.text:
• Supervised Learning → Learns from labeled data (has an answer key) → predicts outcomes.
  • Unsupervised Learning → Learns from unlabeled data → finds hidden patterns/groups on its own.
  • Reinforcement Learning → Learns by trial and error using rewards and penalties → finds the best action/strategy.

docs.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol) — From Scratch to Advanced
docs.text: Simple notes on MCP — the "USB-C for AI" that lets AI models connect to real tools and data.

docs.title: 1. The Problem Before MCP
docs.text:
AI models like Claude/GPT are great at thinking and generating text, but by themselves they are stuck inside a chat box — they can't: - Check your actual Gmail - Look at your Google Drive files - Check today's real weather - Update a Notion page - Query your company's database

To connect an AI to each of these tools, developers had to build a custom, one-off integration for every single tool, for every single AI model.

docs.title: The Old Way (Messy)
docs.text:
ChatGPT ↔ custom code ↔ Gmail
ChatGPT ↔ custom code ↔ Notion
Claude  ↔ custom code ↔ Gmail       (built again, separately!)
Claude  ↔ custom code ↔ Notion      (built again, separately!)

Every AI needed its own separate connector for every tool — lots of duplicate work, hard to maintain.

docs.title: 2. What is MCP?
docs.text:
Simple definition: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard (created by Anthropic) that defines one common way for AI models to connect to external tools, apps, and data sources — instead of everyone building custom, one-off connections.

Simple analogy: USB-C. Before USB-C, every device had a different charging port/cable. USB-C became one universal standard — now any USB-C device works with any USB-C cable/charger. MCP does the same thing for connecting AI to tools — build one MCP connector for Gmail, and ANY MCP-compatible AI (Claude, or others) can use it.

docs.title: The New Way (Clean, with MCP)
docs.text:
Gmail  → MCP Server ─┐
Notion → MCP Server ─┼──→ MCP (standard connection) ──→ Any AI model (Claude, etc.)
Slack  → MCP Server ─┘

Build the connector once, and it works with any AI that supports MCP — no need to rebuild it for every model.

docs.title: 3. Core Building Blocks of MCP
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning MCP Server A small program that connects to a specific tool/data source (e.g., Gmail, GitHub, a database) and exposes it in a standard way MCP Client The AI application (like Claude) that connects to MCP servers to use their tools Tools Specific actions the server offers (e.g., "send_email," "search_files," "create_task") Resources Data the server can provide to the model (e.g., a document, a database record) Prompts Pre-written prompt templates the server can offer for common tasks

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Think of an MCP Server for Gmail: - Tools it exposes: send_email, search_inbox, read_email - Resources it exposes: the actual email content/threads - Claude (the MCP client) can now call these tools directly — e.g., "search my inbox for invoices from last month" — because the Gmail MCP server understands and handles that request.

docs.title: 4. How MCP Works (Step-by-Step, Simplified)
docs.text: Step What Happens 1. Connection The AI app (client) connects to an MCP server (e.g., a Gmail MCP server) 2. Discovery The client asks the server: "What tools/resources do you offer?" 3. Request Based on the user's request ("check my unread emails"), the AI decides to call a specific tool (search_inbox) 4. Execution The MCP server actually performs the action (searches Gmail) and returns real data 5. Response The AI takes that real data and uses it to generate a helpful answer for the user

docs.title: Example (Full Flow)
docs.text:
You ask Claude: "Do I have any unread emails from my boss today?"

  1. Claude (client) connects to the Gmail MCP server
  2. Claude sees the server offers a search_inbox tool
  3. Claude calls search_inbox with filters (unread, sender = boss, today)
  4. The Gmail MCP server actually searches your real inbox and returns results
  5. Claude reads the results and replies: "Yes, you have 2 unread emails from [boss] today..."

Without MCP, Claude would have no way to actually check your real inbox — it would just generate a generic, made-up-sounding response (potential hallucination!). This is exactly the same "look-up-then-answer" idea you learned in RAG — MCP is one of the ways an AI actually performs the "look-up" part on real, live tools instead of documents.

docs.title: 5. Why MCP Matters (Key Benefits)
docs.text: Benefit Explanation One standard, many tools Build a connector once — works across any MCP-supporting AI Faster development No need to rebuild custom integrations for every AI model separately Real, live actions AI can perform actual actions (send emails, book meetings) — not just talk about them Reduces hallucination AI can pull real, current data instead of guessing Growing ecosystem Since it's an open standard, many companies build MCP servers for their own products

docs.title: 6. Where MCP Fits with What You've Already Learned
docs.text:
RAG            → AI looks up documents/knowledge before answering (read-only, mostly)
MCP            → AI connects to real tools & live data sources in a standardized way
AI Agents      → Use tools (via MCP or similar) to perform tasks
Agentic AI     → Uses MULTIPLE tools/MCP servers together, planning multi-step actions independently

In short: MCP is often the "plumbing" that makes AI Agents and Agentic AI actually able to do things in the real world — checking your calendar, sending a message, running a search — instead of just generating text about it.

docs.title: 7. Real-World Examples of MCP in Use
docs.text: MCP Server Example What It Lets the AI Do Google Drive MCP Search/read your files and documents GitHub MCP Check issues, pull requests, repositories Slack MCP Read/send messages in specific channels Database MCP Query and retrieve records from a company database Calendar MCP Check availability, create/update events Web Search / Browser MCP Search the internet and browse pages live

docs.title: 8. Key Terms (Quick Glossary — Full List)
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning MCP Model Context Protocol — a universal standard connecting AI models to tools/data MCP Server Program exposing a specific tool/data source in the MCP standard format MCP Client The AI app (e.g., Claude) that uses MCP servers Tool A specific action an MCP server offers (e.g., send_email) Resource Data an MCP server can provide to the AI Connector Common term for an MCP server built for a specific app/service Open Standard A publicly available specification anyone can build with/for — not owned by one company

docs.title: One-Line Summary (for quick revision)
docs.text:
• MCP → A universal standard ("USB-C for AI") that lets AI models connect to real tools/data in one consistent way.
  • Before MCP → Every AI needed a separate, custom-built connector for every tool (messy, repeated work).
  • With MCP → Build a connector once → works with any MCP-supporting AI.
  • Why it matters → Lets AI perform real actions (not just talk), reduces hallucination by using live data, and powers modern AI Agents/Agentic AI systems.

docs.title: Memory in Agents — Complete Notes
docs.text: Memory = Agent/LLM ka woh mechanism jisse wo purani conversation, facts, ya experiences yaad rakh sakta hai — taaki har interaction "fresh start" na ho, aur context continuity bani rahe.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Why Memory is Needed
  2. The Core Problem — LLMs are Stateless
  3. Types of Memory
  4. Short-Term Memory (Conversation Buffer)
  5. Long-Term Memory
  6. Summarization Memory
  7. Entity Memory
  8. Episodic vs Semantic vs Procedural Memory
  9. Memory Storage Options
  10. How Memory Fits into an Agent's Loop
  11. Context Window Limitations & Memory Management
  12. Best Practices
  13. Common Mistakes
  14. Cheat Sheet

docs.title: 1. Why Memory is Needed
docs.text:
Bina memory ke, har baar jab aap LLM se baat karte ho, wo bilkul naye insaan ki tarah react karega — usse pichli baatcheet ka kuch bhi yaad nahi rahega.

Analogy: Socho aap ek doctor se baat kar rahe ho jisko har 2 minute me amnesia ho jata hai — har baar aapko apni poori medical history dobara batani padegi. Memory iss problem ko solve karti hai — doctor (LLM) ko aapki history yaad rehti hai across the conversation (aur kabhi-kabhi across multiple sessions bhi).

docs.title: 2. The Core Problem — LLMs are Stateless
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: LLMs khud se kuch bhi yaad nahi rakhte — har API call independent hoti hai. Model ko sirf wahi pata hota hai jo aap current request me bhejte ho (prompt ke andar).

Request 1: "My name is Rahul." → Response: "Nice to meet you, Rahul!"
Request 2 (NEW, separate call): "What's my name?" → Response: "I don't know your name" 
   (kyunki Request 1 ka context is naye call me include hi nahi kiya gaya)

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
Har naye request ke saath, poori (ya relevant) purani conversation history ko bhi wapas bhejna padta hai:

Request 2 (with memory): 
   [Previous: "My name is Rahul." "Nice to meet you, Rahul!"] 
   + New message: "What's my name?"
→ Response: "Your name is Rahul!"

Key Insight: Memory asal me LLM ke andar "store" nahi hoti — balki developer/system purani history ko track karta hai aur har naye request ke saath dobara bhejta hai. LLM sirf jo "context window" me hai, wahi "yaad" rakh pata hai.

docs.title: 3. Types of Memory
docs.text: Type Duration Purpose Short-Term Memory Ek hi conversation/session tak Current chat ka context maintain karna Long-Term Memory Multiple sessions ke across User preferences, past interactions yaad rakhna Summarization Memory Compressed version of long conversations Lambi history ko chhota, useful summary me convert karna Entity Memory Specific facts about people/things "User ka naam Rahul hai, wo Mumbai me rehta hai" jaisi facts track karna

docs.title: 4. Short-Term Memory (Conversation Buffer)
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Current conversation ke saare (ya recent) messages ko as-is store karke, har naye request ke saath bhej dena.

docs.title: Conversation Buffer (Full History)
docs.text:
conversation = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "My name is Rahul."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Nice to meet you, Rahul!"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What's my name?"}
]
# Poori history LLM ko bhej do
  • ✅ Simple, sabse accurate (kuch bhi miss nahi hota)
  • ❌ Context window limit ka problem — bahut lambi conversation me, purane messages ki wajah se token limit exceed ho sakta hai (aur cost bhi badhta hai)

docs.title: Conversation Buffer Window (Sliding Window)
docs.text:
Sirf last N messages (e.g., last 10) rakho, purane automatically drop kar do.
  • ✅ Token usage control me rehta hai
  • ❌ Bahut purani important info permanently lost ho sakti hai

docs.title: 5. Long-Term Memory
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Information jo current session ke bahar bhi persist karti hai — agli baar jab user wapas aaye (naya session), tab bhi yeh yaad rahe.

docs.title: Example Use Cases
docs.text:
• User preferences: "Mujhe short answers pasand hain" (ek baar bataya, hamesha yaad rahe)
  • Past interactions: "Pichli baar humne X topic discuss kiya tha"
  • Personal facts: "User ka favorite programming language Python hai"

docs.title: How It's Implemented
docs.text:
• Conversation ke important facts ko extract karke ek database (vector DB ya normal DB) me store kiya jata hai.
  • Naye session me, relevant facts retrieve karke context me include kiye jate hain (RAG jaisa hi concept!).
New Session Starts
   │
   ▼
Retrieve relevant long-term memories (from DB) about this user
   │
   ▼
Inject into system prompt/context: "User previously mentioned: prefers Python, works in finance..."
   │
   ▼
Continue conversation with this added context

docs.title: 6. Summarization Memory
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Poori conversation history store karne ke bajaye, LLM se hi periodically summarize karwate raho — taaki lambi conversation bhi ek chhoti summary me fit ho jaye.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
After every N messages:
   → Send full recent conversation to LLM
   → Ask: "Summarize this conversation so far in 3-4 sentences"
   → Replace the full history with this summary
   → Continue conversation using [Summary] + [New Messages]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Original History (500 messages about a coding project)
   ↓ (summarized)
Summary: "User is building a Python web app using FastAPI. They've discussed 
database schema design and are now working on authentication. Prefers concise code examples."
  • ✅ Token usage bahut kam ho jata hai lambi conversations me
  • ❌ Kuch specific details summary me lost ho sakte hain (trade-off hai)

docs.title: 7. Entity Memory
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Conversation se specific entities (people, places, things, facts) ko track karke ek structured format me store karna.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "user_name": "Rahul",
  "location": "Mumbai",
  "occupation": "Software Engineer",
  "current_project": "E-commerce recommendation system",
  "preferences": ["concise answers", "Python code examples"]
}
  • ✅ Structured hone ki wajah se precise retrieval possible hai (e.g., "user ka naam kya hai" — seedha field se mil jayega)
  • ✅ Conversation buffer ke comparison me bahut compact

docs.title: 8. Episodic vs Semantic vs Procedural Memory (Advanced Categorization)
docs.text:
Yeh categorization human memory se inspired hai, advanced agent systems me use hoti hai:

Type Meaning Example Episodic Memory Specific past events/interactions "Last week, user asked about refunds and was upset" Semantic Memory General facts/knowledge about the user or world "User works in finance", "User prefers metric units" Procedural Memory How to do things — learned patterns/skills "This user always wants responses in bullet points"

Yeh distinction especially advanced/production-grade AI assistants me use hoti hai (jaise personal AI assistants jo long-term relationship maintain karte hain).

docs.title: 9. Memory Storage Options
docs.text:
Storage Type Use Case In-memory (RAM) Simple, single-session apps, testing (data lost on restart) Redis Fast, temporary session storage — good for short-term memory SQL/NoSQL Database Structured long-term memory (entity facts, user profiles) Vector Database Long-term memory jisme semantic search chahiye (e.g., "find similar past conversations")

LangGraph me humne Checkpointer (MemorySaver, SqliteSaver, PostgresSaver) dekha tha — yeh exactly isi purpose ke liye hai: state/memory ko persist karna.

docs.title: 10. How Memory Fits into an Agent's Loop
docs.text:
User sends new message
        │
        ▼
Retrieve relevant memory:
   - Short-term: recent conversation buffer
   - Long-term: relevant facts/past interactions (via DB/vector search)
        │
        ▼
Combine: [System Prompt] + [Long-term Memory] + [Short-term History] + [New Message]
        │
        ▼
Send to LLM → Generate Response
        │
        ▼
Update Memory:
   - Add new message to short-term buffer
   - Extract any new important facts → save to long-term memory
   - If buffer too long → summarize

docs.title: 11. Context Window Limitations & Memory Management
docs.text: Problem: LLMs ki context window limited hoti hai (e.g., 200K tokens) — poori history hamesha nahi bhej sakte, especially long-running agents/conversations me.

docs.title: Strategies to Manage This
docs.text:
Strategy How It Works Sliding Window Sirf last N messages rakho Summarization Purani history ko summary me compress karo Selective Retrieval (RAG-style) Poori history store karo (DB me), lekin sirf relevant parts retrieve karke context me daalo Hierarchical Memory Recent messages = full detail; older messages = summarized; very old = just key facts

Most production systems use a hybrid approach: Recent messages full detail me rakhte hain (short-term buffer), aur purani/important info ko summarized ya entity-based long-term memory me store karte hain.

docs.title: 12. Best Practices
docs.text: Practice Why Use sliding window + summarization together Balance between context richness and token cost Extract and store only "important" facts long-term Avoid bloating memory with irrelevant chit-chat Use vector search for long-term memory retrieval Ensures only relevant past info is pulled in, not everything Regularly test memory accuracy Make sure agent isn't "forgetting" or "hallucinating" facts about the user Give users control over their memory Let users view/edit/delete what the system remembers about them (privacy)

docs.title: 13. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix Sending entire raw history every time Token cost explodes, hits context limit eventually Use summarization or sliding window No long-term memory at all User has to repeat preferences/info every session Implement entity/long-term memory for persistent apps Storing everything without filtering Memory becomes cluttered with irrelevant info Extract only meaningful facts, not every message Not handling memory conflicts (contradicting facts over time) Agent might use outdated/wrong info Update/overwrite facts when new info contradicts old Ignoring privacy/security of stored memory Sensitive user data at risk Encrypt stored memory, give users deletion controls

docs.title: One-Line Memory Tricks
docs.text:
• Short-Term Memory → "Current conversation yaad rakhna"
  • Long-Term Memory → "Sessions ke paar bhi yaad rakhna"
  • Summarization Memory → "Lambi baat ko chhota summary bana do"
  • Entity Memory → "Specific facts ko structured format me store karo"
  • LLMs are Stateless → "Har request independent hai — memory developer manage karta hai, LLM khud nahi"

docs.title: Quick Recap Flow
docs.text:
Conversation Happens
   │
   ▼
Short-Term: Add to buffer (or summarize if too long)
   │
   ▼
Extract Important Facts → Save to Long-Term Memory (DB)
   │
   ▼
Next Interaction: Retrieve relevant memory → Inject into context → Continue

docs.title: Golden Rule
docs.text: "LLMs don't remember anything on their own — memory is an engineering layer YOU build around the model, deciding what to keep, summarize, or discard."

docs.title: Multi-Agent Systems — Complete Notes
docs.text: Multi-Agent System = Ek se zyada AI agents jo mil kar ek complex task solve karte hain — har agent ka apna specific role/specialization hota hai, jaise ek team me alag-alag experts kaam karte hain.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Why Multi-Agent Systems are Needed
  2. Single Agent vs Multi-Agent — The Core Difference
  3. Core Multi-Agent Architectures
  4. Supervisor (Orchestrator) Pattern — Deep Dive
  5. Network (Peer-to-Peer) Pattern — Deep Dive
  6. Hierarchical Pattern — Deep Dive
  7. Sequential/Pipeline Pattern — Deep Dive
  8. Agent Communication — How Agents "Talk" to Each Other
  9. Shared State vs Isolated State
  10. Real-World Examples
  11. Challenges in Multi-Agent Systems
  12. When to Use Multi-Agent vs Single Agent
  13. Common Mistakes
  14. Cheat Sheet

docs.title: 1. Why Multi-Agent Systems are Needed
docs.text:
Ek single agent ko bahut saari cheezein ek saath acchi tarah karne ko bolna difficult hota hai — jaise ek insaan se expect karna ki wo doctor, lawyer, aur accountant teeno ka kaam ek saath perfectly kare.

Problem with a single "do everything" agent: - Prompt bahut complex aur overloaded ho jata hai (bahut saare instructions, tools, edge cases) - Agent confuse ho sakta hai ki kaunsa context/tool kab relevant hai - Debugging mushkil ho jati hai (sab kuch ek hi jagah mixed hai)

Solution: Task ko specialized agents me todo — har agent apna ek clear responsibility rakhta hai, aur wo mil kar poora kaam complete karte hain.

Analogy: Socho ek hospital — ek hi doctor se expect nahi karte ki wo surgery bhi kare, X-ray bhi padhe, aur medicine bhi dispense kare. Instead: Surgeon, Radiologist, aur Pharmacist — har ek apna specialized kaam karta hai, aur ek coordinator (head doctor/nurse) unke beech information pass karta hai. Multi-Agent Systems bilkul isi tarah kaam karte hain.

docs.title: 2. Single Agent vs Multi-Agent — The Core Difference
docs.text: Feature Single Agent Multi-Agent System Responsibility Ek hi agent sab kuch handle karta hai Har agent ek specific role/task handle karta hai Complexity Handling Simple to moderate tasks ke liye theek Complex, multi-domain tasks ke liye better Prompt Size Bada, sab instructions ek jagah Chhota, focused prompts per agent Debugging Ek hi jagah dekhna hai, lekin messy ho sakta hai complex tasks me Har agent ka kaam alag se trace kiya ja sakta hai Coordination Overhead Nahi hoti Agents ke beech communication/handoff manage karna padta hai Cost Kam (ek hi LLM call chain) Zyada (multiple agents = multiple LLM calls)

docs.title: 3. Core Multi-Agent Architectures
docs.text: Pattern Simple Idea Supervisor (Orchestrator) Ek "manager" agent decide karta hai kaunsa worker agent kab kaam karega Network (Peer-to-Peer) Agents directly ek doosre ko call kar sakte hain, koi central manager nahi Hierarchical Multiple layers of supervisors — bade supervisor ke neeche chhote supervisors, unke neeche workers Sequential/Pipeline Agents ek fixed order me kaam karte hain, ek ke baad doosra

docs.title: 4. Supervisor (Orchestrator) Pattern — Deep Dive
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Ek "Supervisor" agent hota hai jo user ke request ko analyze karta hai aur decide karta hai ki kaunsa specialized "Worker" agent iss kaam ko handle karega. Worker apna kaam poora karke result wapas Supervisor ko deta hai, jo agla decision leta hai.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. User Request → Supervisor
2. Supervisor analyzes: "This needs research first"
3. Supervisor routes to → Researcher Agent
4. Researcher completes task → Returns result to Supervisor
5. Supervisor analyzes: "Now I need code written based on this research"
6. Supervisor routes to → Coder Agent
7. Coder completes task → Returns result to Supervisor
8. Supervisor decides: "Task complete" → Returns final answer to user

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
User: "Research the top 3 AI frameworks in 2026 and write a comparison blog post."

Supervisor: "This needs 2 steps: research, then writing."
   → Calls Researcher Agent → Gets data on top 3 frameworks
   → Calls Writer Agent (with research data) → Gets final blog post
Supervisor → Returns final blog post to user

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Clear control flow — easy to understand and debug
  • ✅ Central point of decision-making (predictable routing logic)

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• ❌ Supervisor can become a bottleneck if logic gets complex
  • ❌ All communication routes through supervisor (extra hop = extra latency)

docs.title: 5. Network (Peer-to-Peer) Pattern — Deep Dive
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Koi central "manager" nahi hota — agents directly ek doosre ko call/handoff kar sakte hain based on need.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Har agent ko pata hota hai ki kaunse doosre agents available hain.
  • Agent khud decide karta hai ki uska kaam complete karne ke baad, kis doosre agent ko handoff karna hai (agar zaroorat ho).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Agent A (Customer Query Classifier): "Yeh billing-related query hai" 
   → Directly hands off to → Agent B (Billing Specialist)

Agent B: "Isme technical issue bhi hai" 
   → Directly hands off to → Agent C (Technical Support)

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Zyada flexible — koi rigid central control nahi
  • ✅ Direct communication se latency kam ho sakti hai (ek extra hop skip)

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• ❌ Harder to predict/debug — flow kaafi dynamic ho sakta hai
  • ❌ Agents ke beech "infinite handoff loops" ka risk (A→B→C→A→...)

docs.title: 6. Hierarchical Pattern — Deep Dive
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Multiple layers of supervisors — jaise ek badi company ka organizational chart. Top-level supervisor bade decisions leta hai aur sub-supervisors ko tasks assign karta hai, jo aage apne workers ko manage karte hain.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Bahut bade, complex systems ke liye — jaise ek "AI company" simulate karna jisme multiple departments hain, har department ke apne workers hain.
  • Large-scale enterprise automation jahan tasks naturally departments me divide hote hain.

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Bahut scalable — naye departments/teams easily add ho sakte hain
  • ✅ Complex organizational logic ko naturally model karta hai

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• ❌ Sabse zyada complex to build and maintain
  • ❌ Latency badh sakti hai (multiple layers se guzarna padta hai)

docs.title: 7. Sequential/Pipeline Pattern — Deep Dive
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Agents ek fixed, predetermined order me kaam karte hain — Agent A ka output, Agent B ka input banta hai, jo aage Agent C ko jata hai, waghera.

docs.title: Architecture Diagram
docs.text:
Agent A → Agent B → Agent C → Final Output
(Research)  (Analyze)  (Write)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Agent A (Data Collector): Scrapes latest market data
   → Output: Raw data
Agent B (Analyst): Analyzes the raw data, extracts trends
   → Output: Analysis summary
Agent C (Report Writer): Writes a polished report using the analysis
   → Output: Final Report

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Predictable — sabse simple pattern samajhne/debug karne ke liye
  • ✅ Chain jaisa hi hai, lekin har step ek "full agent" hai (apne khud ke tools/reasoning ke saath)

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• ❌ Kam flexible — agar beech me kuch unexpected ho, pipeline adapt nahi kar sakta easily
  • ❌ Dynamic decision-making (jaise "kaunsa agent next chalega based on situation") support nahi karta

docs.title: 8. Agent Communication — How Agents "Talk" to Each Other
docs.text:
Agents ke beech information pass karne ke common tareeke:

Method How It Works Shared State Object Sab agents ek common "state" (jaise LangGraph ka State) read/write karte hain Direct Message Passing Ek agent ka output text/JSON ke roop me directly doosre agent ko diya jata hai Shared Memory/Database Agents ek common database/vector store me read-write karte hain, isse asynchronously bhi communicate ho sakta hai

docs.title: Example (Shared State — LangGraph Style)
docs.text:
class MultiAgentState(TypedDict):
    research_data: str
    code: str
    final_report: str

# Researcher Agent updates "research_data"
# Coder Agent reads "research_data", updates "code"
# Writer Agent reads both, updates "final_report"

docs.title: 9. Shared State vs Isolated State
docs.text: Approach Description Tradeoff Shared State Sab agents ek hi state object access karte hain Simple to coordinate, lekin agents ek doosre ka data accidentally overwrite kar sakte hain (reducers use karo — pichli LangGraph notes yaad karo) Isolated State Har agent apna khud ka state maintain karta hai, sirf specific outputs share hote hain Zyada modular/safe, lekin communication design karna padta hai explicitly

docs.title: 10. Real-World Examples
docs.text: Example Multi-Agent Setup Software Development Team Simulation Product Manager Agent → Architect Agent → Coder Agent → Tester Agent Content Creation Pipeline Researcher Agent → Writer Agent → Editor Agent → SEO Optimizer Agent Customer Support System Classifier Agent → Specialist Agent (billing/technical/general) → Escalation Agent (if needed) Financial Analysis Data Collector Agent → Risk Analyzer Agent → Report Generator Agent

docs.title: 11. Challenges in Multi-Agent Systems
docs.text: Challenge Description Coordination Overhead Managing communication between agents adds complexity Cost Multiple agents = multiple LLM calls = higher cost than single agent Latency More agents/handoffs = slower overall response time Error Propagation Agar ek agent galti kare, downstream agents bhi affected honge Debugging Complexity Tracing exactly which agent did what, and why, requires good observability tools Infinite Handoff Loops Especially in Network pattern — agents keep passing task to each other without resolution

docs.title: 12. When to Use Multi-Agent vs Single Agent
docs.text:
Situation Recommended Simple, well-defined task Single Agent (simpler, cheaper, faster) Task naturally has distinct specialized phases (research → code → write) Multi-Agent (Pipeline/Supervisor) Need different "expertise"/tools for different sub-tasks Multi-Agent Budget/latency very constrained Single Agent (avoid multi-agent overhead) Building something like an "AI company" simulation or complex enterprise automation Multi-Agent (Hierarchical) Task requires dynamic collaboration without fixed order Multi-Agent (Network)

Practical Advice: Start with a single agent. Only move to multi-agent when you clearly see the single agent's prompt/logic becoming too overloaded or unclear — multi-agent adds real complexity and cost, so it should be justified by the task's actual needs.

docs.title: 13. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix Using multi-agent for simple tasks Unnecessary cost and complexity Use single agent unless task truly needs specialization No clear role boundaries between agents Agents overlap/conflict in responsibilities Define clear, distinct roles for each agent No limit on agent handoffs Risk of infinite loops between agents Set max handoff/iteration limits Poor communication design (unstructured text passing) Information gets lost or misinterpreted between agents Use structured formats (JSON/shared state) for inter-agent communication No observability/tracing Impossible to debug which agent caused an issue Use tracing tools (LangSmith, etc.) to monitor every agent's actions

docs.title: One-Line Memory Tricks
docs.text:
• Supervisor Pattern → "Manager decide karta hai kaunsa worker kab chalega"
  • Network Pattern → "Agents directly ek doosre ko handoff karte hain"
  • Hierarchical Pattern → "Multiple layers of managers, jaise company ka org chart"
  • Sequential/Pipeline → "Fixed order me, ek ke baad doosra"

docs.title: Quick Decision Guide
docs.text:
Simple task → Single Agent
Fixed multi-step process → Sequential Pipeline
Need central control/routing → Supervisor Pattern
Need flexible, dynamic collaboration → Network Pattern
Very large, complex system with departments → Hierarchical Pattern

docs.title: Golden Rule
docs.text: "Multi-Agent Systems are like a well-organized team — each member has a clear job, and the coordination method (supervisor, network, hierarchy, or pipeline) determines how smoothly they work together."

docs.title: Neural Networks & Deep Learning — Basics
docs.text: Simple notes to understand how AI actually "learns" inside.

docs.title: 1. What is a Neural Network?
docs.text:
Simple definition: A Neural Network is a computer system inspired by the human brain. It's made of small units called neurons, connected together in layers, that learn patterns from data.

Just like your brain has neurons that pass signals to each other to help you recognize a face or understand a sentence, a neural network has artificial neurons that pass numbers to each other to learn patterns.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Imagine teaching a child to recognize a cat: - You show many pictures of cats and say "cat" - You show pictures of dogs and say "not cat" - After seeing enough examples, the child learns to recognize a cat on their own

A neural network learns the same way — by seeing lots of examples (data) and adjusting itself until it gets good at the task.

docs.title: 2. Structure of a Neural Network (3 Main Layers)
docs.text:
Layer What it does Example Input Layer Takes in the raw data Pixels of a cat image Hidden Layer(s) Finds patterns step by step Edges → shapes → ears → whiskers Output Layer Gives the final answer "This is a Cat" (95% confident)

The more hidden layers a network has, the "deeper" it is — this is where the term Deep Learning comes from.

docs.title: 3. What is Deep Learning?
docs.text:
Simple definition: Deep Learning = Neural Networks with many hidden layers (deep = many layers), able to learn very complex patterns.

  • Machine Learning (general) → computer learns from data
  • Deep Learning (specific type of ML) → computer learns using multi-layered neural networks, especially good with images, text, audio, and video

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• Simple ML: Predicting house price using a formula based on size and location
  • Deep Learning: Recognizing a face in a photo, translating a sentence, or generating an image — tasks too complex for simple formulas

docs.title: 4. How Does It "Learn"? (In Very Simple Words)
docs.text:
1. Guess – Network makes a prediction (usually wrong at first)
  2. Check the mistake – Compares its guess to the correct answer (this is called loss/error)
  3. Adjust itself – Slightly changes its internal numbers (called weights) to reduce the mistake
  4. Repeat – Does this millions of times with lots of data until it gets accurate

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Teaching the network to recognize "cat" vs "dog": - Round 1: Shows a cat photo → network says "dog" ❌ → it adjusts itself - Round 500: Shows a cat photo → network says "cat" ✅ - After thousands of rounds, it becomes very accurate

This adjusting process is called Training, and the method used to adjust is called Backpropagation (just remember: "it learns from its mistakes, step by step").

docs.title: 5. Key Terms (Quick Glossary)
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning Neuron A small unit that processes a number and passes it forward Weight A number that shows how important a connection is (adjusted during learning) Layer A group of neurons working at one level Training The process of teaching the network using data Dataset The collection of examples used to teach the network Model The trained neural network — the "finished product" Epoch One full pass through the entire training dataset

docs.title: 6. Real-Life Examples of Neural Networks in Action
docs.text: Application What it does Face unlock on phone Recognizes your face using a neural network Netflix/YouTube recommendations Predicts what you'll want to watch Google Translate Converts one language to another Self-driving cars Recognizes roads, signs, pedestrians ChatGPT / Claude Uses a deep neural network (Transformer) to understand & generate text

docs.title: Quick Comparison (Where This Fits)
docs.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI)
   └── Machine Learning (ML)
          └── Deep Learning (DL)
                 └── Neural Networks (the actual structure used)
  • AI → the big goal: machines acting smart
  • ML → machines learning from data instead of being manually programmed
  • Deep Learning → ML using multi-layered neural networks
  • Neural Network → the actual brain-like structure that makes deep learning possible

docs.title: One-Line Summary (for quick revision)
docs.text:
• Neural Network → Brain-inspired structure of connected neurons that learns patterns.
  • Deep Learning → Neural networks with many hidden layers, used for complex tasks (images, text, speech).
  • Training → The network learns by guessing, checking mistakes, and adjusting itself repeatedly.

docs.title: Observability for LLM Apps — Complete Notes
docs.text: Observability = LLM application ke andar kya ho raha hai, yeh dekhne, track karne, aur debug karne ki capability — kaunsa prompt gaya, kaunsa tool call hua, kitna time laga, kitna cost aaya, aur kahan galti hui.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Why Observability is Needed
  2. The Core Problem — LLM Apps are "Black Boxes"
  3. What Observability Tracks (Core Concepts)
  4. Tracing — Deep Dive
  5. Spans — Building Blocks of a Trace
  6. Popular Observability Tools
  7. LangSmith Overview
  8. Langfuse Overview
  9. Key Metrics to Monitor in Production
  10. Debugging Workflow Using Traces
  11. Observability + Evaluation (Connecting the Dots)
  12. Common Mistakes
  13. Cheat Sheet

docs.title: 1. Why Observability is Needed
docs.text:
Jab aapka RAG pipeline ya Agent production me chal raha hota hai, aur koi user complain kare "mujhe galat answer mila", tab bina observability ke aap andhere me tir chala rahe ho — pata hi nahi chalega: - Kaunsi query thi? - Kaunse chunks retrieve hue the? - LLM ne kya reasoning ki? - Kaunsa tool call hua, kya result aaya? - Kahan exactly problem hui — retrieval me, ya generation me?

Analogy: Socho ek car ka dashboard — bina dashboard ke, aapko pata hi nahi chalega ki fuel kitna hai, engine ka temperature kya hai, ya koi warning light on hai ya nahi. Observability tools LLM apps ke liye exactly wahi dashboard provide karte hain.

docs.title: 2. The Core Problem — LLM Apps are "Black Boxes"
docs.text:
Complex RAG/Agent pipelines me bahut saare steps hote hain:

User Query → Query Rewriting → Retrieval → Reranking → Prompt Construction 
→ LLM Call → Tool Call (maybe) → Another LLM Call → Final Response

Bina observability ke, aapko sirf final output dikhta hai — beech ke saare steps "hidden" rehte hain. Agar answer galat aaya, aapko pata nahi chalega kis step pe problem thi.

docs.title: 3. What Observability Tracks (Core Concepts)
docs.text: Concept What It Captures Traces Ek poori request ka end-to-end journey (start se end tak) Spans Trace ke andar individual steps (e.g., "retrieval step", "LLM call step") Latency Har step aur poori request me kitna time laga Token Usage/Cost Har LLM call me kitne tokens use hue, kitna cost aaya Inputs/Outputs Har step ka exact input aur output (prompt, retrieved chunks, LLM response) Errors/Exceptions Kahan errors/failures hue Metadata Extra context — user ID, session ID, model version, etc.

docs.title: 4. Tracing — Deep Dive
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Trace = Ek single user request ka poora record — usme shamil har step, uska input/output, time liya gaya, aur koi error — sab kuch ek jagah, visually organized.

docs.title: Example Trace (Conceptual)
docs.text:
TRACE ID: abc-123 (User asked: "What's our refund policy?")

├── Span 1: Query Embedding
│   Input: "What's our refund policy?"
│   Output: [0.23, -0.11, ...] (embedding vector)
│   Duration: 45ms
│
├── Span 2: Vector Search
│   Input: [embedding vector]
│   Output: [Chunk A, Chunk B, Chunk C] (top-3 retrieved)
│   Duration: 80ms
│
├── Span 3: Reranking
│   Input: [Chunk A, Chunk B, Chunk C]
│   Output: [Chunk B, Chunk A, Chunk C] (reordered)
│   Duration: 120ms
│
├── Span 4: LLM Generation
│   Input: Prompt with [Chunk B, Chunk A, Chunk C] + question
│   Output: "Our refund policy allows returns within 30 days..."
│   Tokens: 450 input, 80 output
│   Cost: $0.002
│   Duration: 850ms
│
Total Trace Duration: 1095ms
Total Cost: $0.002

Iss trace ko dekh ke, agar answer galat tha, aap exactly identify kar sakte ho ki problem retrieval me thi (galat chunks retrieve hue) ya generation me (LLM ne chunks ko misinterpret kiya).

docs.title: 5. Spans — Building Blocks of a Trace
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Span = Trace ka ek individual step/operation. Ek trace me multiple nested spans ho sakte hain (jaise ek span ke andar doosra span, agar wo step aage complex sub-steps me divide ho).

docs.title: Nested Spans Example
docs.text:
Trace: "Agent completes research task"
├── Span: "Understand Query"
├── Span: "Tool Call: Web Search"
│    ├── Sub-span: "API Request"
│    └── Sub-span: "Parse Results"
├── Span: "LLM Reasoning"
└── Span: "Generate Final Answer"

Yeh hierarchical structure especially useful hai Agent/Multi-step workflows (jaise LangGraph agents) debug karne ke liye — aap exactly dekh sakte ho ki agent ne kaunse steps liye, kis order me.

docs.title: 6. Popular Observability Tools
docs.text: Tool Key Features LangSmith LangChain/LangGraph ka native observability tool — tracing, evaluation, dataset management Langfuse Open-source, framework-agnostic — tracing, prompt management, evaluation, cost tracking Weights & Biases (W&B) Prompts Tracing + experiment tracking, popular in ML-heavy teams Helicone Lightweight, proxy-based observability — easy to integrate Arize Phoenix Open-source, strong focus on LLM evaluation + observability together

docs.title: 7. LangSmith Overview
docs.text: Simple Meaning: LangChain ka official observability platform — agar aap LangChain/LangGraph use kar rahe ho, yeh sabse seamless integration deta hai (kam se kam extra code chahiye hota hai).

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Automatic Tracing: LangChain/LangGraph calls automatically trace ho jate hain (minimal setup)
  • Dataset Management: Test datasets bana ke, unpe evaluations run kar sakte ho
  • Evaluation: Built-in evaluators (Faithfulness, Correctness, etc.) directly traces pe apply kar sakte ho
  • Prompt Playground: Prompts ko directly UI me test/iterate kar sakte ho
  • Monitoring Dashboards: Latency, cost, error rate — sab visualize kiya ja sakta hai

docs.title: Basic Setup (Conceptual)
docs.text:
import os
os.environ["LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2"] = "true"
os.environ["LANGCHAIN_API_KEY"] = "your-api-key"

# Ab aapke saare LangChain/LangGraph calls automatically LangSmith pe trace honge

docs.title: 8. Langfuse Overview
docs.text: Simple Meaning: Ek open-source, framework-agnostic observability tool — matlab yeh LangChain ke bina bhi (ya kisi bhi framework ke saath) kaam karta hai, aur aap khud host bhi kar sakte ho (self-hosting option, jo privacy-conscious companies ke liye important hai).

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Framework-Agnostic: Kaam karta hai LangChain, LlamaIndex, ya even raw API calls ke saath bhi
  • Self-Hostable: Apna data apne servers pe rakh sakte ho (compliance/privacy ke liye important)
  • Prompt Management: Prompts ko version control ki tarah manage kar sakte ho
  • Cost Tracking: Detailed token usage aur cost breakdown

docs.title: Basic Setup (Conceptual)
docs.text:
from langfuse.decorators import observe

@observe()
def my_rag_pipeline(query: str):
    chunks = retrieve(query)
    response = generate(query, chunks)
    return response

# Yeh function call automatically Langfuse pe trace hoga

docs.title: 9. Key Metrics to Monitor in Production
docs.text:
Metric Why It Matters Latency (p50, p95, p99) Average aur worst-case response times — user experience directly impact karta hai Token Usage Cost directly iske proportional hota hai Cost per Request Business viability track karne ke liye Error Rate Kitni requests fail ho rahi hain (tool errors, LLM errors, timeouts) Retrieval Quality (RAG systems) Kya sahi chunks consistently mil rahe hain production traffic pe bhi User Feedback (thumbs up/down) Real-world signal ki users satisfied hain ya nahi Hallucination Rate Periodic sampling se check karo faithfulness metrics production data pe

p50/p95/p99 ka matlab: p50 = median latency (50% requests isse fast hain), p95 = 95% requests isse fast hain (matlab sirf 5% requests isse slow hain — worst-case ka signal). Production monitoring me p95/p99 dekhna zyada important hota hai average se, kyunki wo "worst user experience" ko highlight karta hai.

docs.title: 10. Debugging Workflow Using Traces
docs.text:
Jab koi issue report ho ("bot ne galat answer diya"), yeh systematic approach follow karo:

1. Find the specific trace (using user ID, timestamp, or session ID)
2. Check the final output — confirm the issue
3. Walk backward through spans:
   a. Was the retrieval step correct? (Check retrieved chunks)
   b. Was reranking correct? (Check reordering)
   c. Was the prompt constructed correctly? (Check final prompt sent to LLM)
   d. Did the LLM misinterpret good context? (Faithfulness issue)
4. Identify the exact failure point
5. Fix that specific component (better chunking, better prompt, etc.)
6. Re-test with the same query to confirm fix

docs.title: 11. Observability + Evaluation (Connecting the Dots)
docs.text:
Observability aur Evaluation (pichli notes) saath me kaam karte hain:

Observability → Collects real production data/traces (what's actually happening)
       │
       ▼
Evaluation → Uses that data to measure quality (Faithfulness, Relevance, etc.)
       │
       ▼
Insights → Identify patterns (e.g., "retrieval fails often for questions about X topic")
       │
       ▼
Improvements → Fix the specific weak points (better chunking for X topic, etc.)

Modern tools (LangSmith, Langfuse) combine both — aap traces collect bhi kar sakte ho aur unpe directly evaluation metrics bhi run kar sakte ho, ek hi platform me.

docs.title: 12. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix No tracing in production Impossible to debug issues when they occur Set up tracing from day one, even in early development Only checking final output, not intermediate steps Miss the actual root cause of failures Always inspect full trace (all spans) when debugging Not monitoring cost/token usage Bills can spiral unexpectedly Set up cost dashboards and alerts Ignoring p95/p99 latency, only looking at averages Miss worst-case user experiences Monitor percentile latencies, not just average Not connecting observability data back to evaluation Miss opportunities to systematically improve the system Periodically sample production traces and run evaluation metrics on them

docs.title: One-Line Memory Tricks
docs.text:
• Observability → "LLM app ka dashboard — dekho andar kya ho raha hai"
  • Trace → "Ek poori request ka safarnama, start se end tak"
  • Span → "Trace ke andar ek individual step"
  • LangSmith → "LangChain ka native observability tool"
  • Langfuse → "Open-source, framework-agnostic, self-hostable observability tool"

docs.title: Quick Recap Flow
docs.text:
User Request → [Every step gets traced: retrieval, reranking, LLM call, tool calls]
   → Trace stored with full input/output/timing/cost
   → When issue occurs: inspect trace → find exact failure point → fix it
   → Periodically: run evaluation metrics on sampled traces to catch systemic issues

docs.title: Golden Rule
docs.text: "You can't fix what you can't see — observability gives you the visibility to debug, optimize cost, and continuously improve your LLM application in production."

docs.title: OpenAI Agents SDK vs LangGraph — Complete Notes
docs.text: OpenAI Agents SDK = OpenAI ka apna lightweight, minimal framework hai agents banane ke liye — simple Python-first design ke saath. LangGraph = Zyada flexible, graph-based framework hai jo complex, custom control flow (loops, branches, multi-agent) ke liye deep control deta hai.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. What is OpenAI Agents SDK
  2. Core Concepts in OpenAI Agents SDK
  3. How OpenAI Agents SDK Works (Example)
  4. What is LangGraph (Quick Recap)
  5. Side-by-Side Comparison
  6. Philosophy Difference — "Opinionated Simplicity" vs "Flexible Control"
  7. When to Use OpenAI Agents SDK
  8. When to Use LangGraph
  9. Can They Be Used Together/Interchanged?
  10. Common Mistakes
  11. Cheat Sheet

docs.title: 1. What is OpenAI Agents SDK
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: OpenAI Agents SDK ek lightweight, production-ready framework hai jo OpenAI ne specifically multi-agent workflows banane ke liye release kiya — iska focus simplicity aur minimal abstractions pe hai (bahut kam "magic"/hidden complexity).

Yeh OpenAI ke pehle ke experimental project "Swarm" ka production-grade successor hai — Swarm ek research/educational prototype tha, Agents SDK usko production-ready banata hai.

docs.title: Core Philosophy
docs.text:
• Minimal core concepts — sirf handful of primitives seekhne padte hain (bahut kam learning curve)
  • Python-first (aur ab TypeScript/JS support bhi hai) — feels like writing normal Python code, not a heavy framework
  • Provider-agnostic — sirf OpenAI models tak limited nahi, dusre LLM providers (via compatible APIs) ke saath bhi use ho sakta hai

docs.title: 2. Core Concepts in OpenAI Agents SDK
docs.text: Concept Simple Meaning Agent Ek LLM + instructions + tools + (optional) handoffs — ek self-contained "worker" Handoffs Ek agent, task ko doosre specialized agent ko transfer kar sakta hai (jaise LangGraph ka multi-agent routing) Tools Functions jo agent call kar sakta hai (same concept jo humne Tool Calling notes me dekha) Guardrails Built-in input/output validation checks (jo humne Guardrails notes me dekha, yahan SDK-native support hai) Sessions Conversation memory/state automatically manage karne ka built-in mechanism Runner Woh component jo agent ko actually execute karta hai (agent loop chalata hai jab tak final answer na mile) Tracing Built-in observability — automatically traces generate hote hain (jaise humne LangSmith/Langfuse notes me dekha)

docs.title: Basic Single Agent
docs.text:
from agents import Agent, Runner

agent = Agent(
    name="Customer Support Agent",
    instructions="You help customers with billing questions.",
    tools=[check_billing_status]  # a Python function decorated as a tool
)

result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "What's my current bill?")
print(result.final_output)

docs.title: Multi-Agent with Handoffs
docs.text:
billing_agent = Agent(
    name="Billing Agent",
    instructions="Handle billing-related questions."
)

technical_agent = Agent(
    name="Technical Support Agent",
    instructions="Handle technical issues."
)

triage_agent = Agent(
    name="Triage Agent",
    instructions="Determine if the query is about billing or technical issues, and hand off accordingly.",
    handoffs=[billing_agent, technical_agent]   # <-- this is the key concept
)

result = Runner.run_sync(triage_agent, "My internet isn't working")
# Triage agent automatically hands off to technical_agent

Notice: Handoffs yahan ek first-class, simple concept hai — bas ek list me doosre agents specify kar do, aur Runner khud manage karta hai ki control kab transfer hoga.

docs.title: 4. What is LangGraph (Quick Recap)
docs.text:
(Humari pichli detailed notes me poora cover ho chuka hai — yahan sirf comparison ke liye recap)

LangGraph ek graph-based framework hai jisme aap explicitly define karte ho: - State (shared data schema, with Reducers) - Nodes (individual steps/functions) - Edges (fixed ya conditional — routing logic) - Aap poora control flow khud design karte ho — loops, branches, parallel paths, sab kuch explicit hota hai.

docs.title: 5. Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text: Feature OpenAI Agents SDK LangGraph Core Abstraction Agent + Handoffs (simple, high-level) State + Nodes + Edges (graph, low-level control) Learning Curve ✅ Low — few concepts to learn ❌ Steeper — need to understand graphs, state, reducers Control Flow Flexibility 🟡 Moderate — handoffs cover common patterns, but less granular control ✅ Very High — full custom loops, conditions, parallel branches possible Multi-Agent Support ✅ Built-in via Handoffs (simple pattern) ✅ Supported, but you build the routing/architecture yourself (Supervisor, Network, etc. — pichli notes) Memory/Sessions ✅ Built-in Sessions feature 🟡 Requires setting up Checkpointer explicitly Tracing/Observability ✅ Built-in tracing out of the box 🟡 Requires integrating LangSmith/Langfuse separately Guardrails ✅ Native, built-in concept 🟡 You implement guardrails yourself (as separate nodes/checks) Provider Lock-in Originally OpenAI-focused, but now supports other providers too Fully provider-agnostic — works with any LLM (Claude, OpenAI, open-source, etc.) Ecosystem/Integrations Smaller, newer, growing Very large — part of LangChain ecosystem, huge number of integrations Best For Quick-to-build, straightforward multi-agent apps Complex, highly custom, production-grade workflows needing fine control

docs.title: 6. Philosophy Difference — "Opinionated Simplicity" vs "Flexible Control"
docs.text: Yeh sabse important conceptual difference hai:

docs.title: OpenAI Agents SDK — "Opinionated Simplicity"
docs.text:
• SDK khud decide karta hai ki agent loop kaise chalega, handoffs kaise kaam karenge.
  • Aapko kam decisions lene padte hain — bas Agent define karo, tools do, handoffs specify karo — baaki SDK handle kar leta hai.
  • Trade-off: Agar aapko kuch bahut custom/unusual control flow chahiye (jaise complex conditional loops, unusual state merging), SDK utna flexible nahi hai.

docs.title: LangGraph — "Flexible, Explicit Control"
docs.text:
• Aap har cheez explicitly define karte ho — state schema, har node, har edge (including conditions).
  • Zyada verbose/complex to set up, lekin kisi bhi tarah ka control flow design kar sakte ho — koi limitation nahi.
  • Trade-off: Zyada code likhna padta hai, zyada seekhna padta hai, lekin unlimited flexibility milti hai.

Analogy: OpenAI Agents SDK ek automatic transmission car jaisa hai — drive karna aasan hai, most situations handle ho jati hain, lekin bahut specific/unusual driving styles ke liye utna control nahi milta. LangGraph ek manual transmission car jaisa hai — seekhna thoda mushkil hai, lekin aap exactly control kar sakte ho ki gear kab badalna hai, kaise drive karna hai — full control.

docs.title: 7. When to Use OpenAI Agents SDK
docs.text: Situation Why Quick prototyping of a multi-agent app Minimal setup, fast to get running Simple triage/handoff patterns (e.g., support bot routing to specialists) Handoffs are a natural fit, no extra engineering needed Want built-in tracing/guardrails without extra integration These come out-of-the-box Team prefers simplicity over granular control Less to learn, less boilerplate code Primarily using OpenAI models Native, first-party support

docs.title: 8. When to Use LangGraph
docs.text: Situation Why Need complex, custom control flow (unusual loops, conditions, parallel branches) Full graph-level control available Building with non-OpenAI models (Claude, open-source, etc.) as primary need Fully provider-agnostic by design Need deep integration with the broader LangChain ecosystem (tons of pre-built integrations) LangGraph is part of that ecosystem Production system requiring fine-grained state management (custom reducers, complex merging logic) LangGraph's explicit State/Reducer system handles this well Building genuinely novel/complex multi-agent architectures (hierarchical, network patterns) More primitives available to construct these from scratch

docs.title: 9. Can They Be Used Together/Interchanged?
docs.text:
• Not typically "together" in the same pipeline — they're alternative choices for building the same kind of thing (agent orchestration).
  • However, you can use OpenAI's models inside a LangGraph application (LangGraph doesn't care which LLM provider you use), and conceptually you could even use LangChain's tools within an OpenAI Agents SDK setup with some glue code — but this isn't the common/intended pattern.
  • Practical reality: Teams usually pick one framework for their agent orchestration layer, based on the tradeoffs above, rather than mixing both in one project.

docs.title: 10. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Problem Fix Choosing LangGraph for a simple triage-style bot Unnecessary complexity for a simple use case Consider OpenAI Agents SDK's Handoffs pattern for simpler needs Choosing OpenAI Agents SDK for a highly custom, complex workflow You may hit its flexibility limits and need to "fight" the framework Use LangGraph when you know you need fine-grained custom control Assuming OpenAI Agents SDK only works with OpenAI models Limits your provider options unnecessarily Check current SDK docs — provider support has been expanding Not evaluating built-in features (tracing, guardrails) before adding third-party tools Redundant tooling, wasted integration effort Check what's already built into your chosen framework first

docs.title: One-Line Memory Tricks
docs.text:
• OpenAI Agents SDK → "Simple, opinionated, batteries-included — Agent + Handoffs"
  • LangGraph → "Flexible, explicit, graph-based — State + Nodes + Edges, full control"

docs.title: Quick Decision Guide
docs.text:
Want simplicity, fast setup, built-in tracing/guardrails → OpenAI Agents SDK
Want maximum flexibility, custom control flow, provider-agnostic → LangGraph

docs.title: Golden Rule
docs.text: "OpenAI Agents SDK trades some flexibility for simplicity and built-in production features. LangGraph trades some simplicity for complete, granular control over your agent's flow. Choose based on how custom your workflow truly needs to be."

docs.title: Overfitting vs Underfitting
docs.text: Simple notes on the two most common training mistakes in Machine Learning.

docs.title: Quick Overview
docs.text: Type What Happens Result Overfitting Model memorizes training data too closely Great on training data, bad on new/real data Underfitting Model doesn't learn enough from training data Bad on both training data and new data

docs.title: 1. Overfitting
docs.text:
Simple definition: When a model memorizes the training data too well — including its noise and random details — instead of learning the general pattern. It performs great on data it has seen, but poorly on new, unseen data.

  • The model becomes too specific to the training examples
  • It fails to generalize to real-world situations

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Imagine a student preparing for an exam by memorizing the exact answers to last year's past paper — word for word — instead of understanding the concepts.

  • On the exact same past paper → scores 100% ✅
  • On the actual new exam (different questions, same topics) → fails ❌, because they never understood the concept, just memorized specific answers

AI Example: A model trained to detect cats is shown 1,000 cat photos, but by coincidence, all the training photos have a red background. - The model might wrongly learn: "red background = cat" - Show it a cat photo with a blue background → it fails to recognize the cat ❌ - It overfit to an irrelevant detail (background color) instead of learning what a cat actually looks like

docs.title: 2. Underfitting
docs.text:
Simple definition: When a model is too simple or hasn't trained enough to even learn the basic pattern in the data — so it performs poorly on both the training data and new data.

  • The model hasn't learned enough
  • It's too simple to capture the real pattern

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Imagine a student who barely studied at all for the exam — didn't even read the basic concepts properly.

  • On practice questions → performs poorly ❌
  • On the actual exam → also performs poorly ❌

Because they never learned the material in the first place — not even the basics.

AI Example: A model trying to predict house prices using only one factor (like "number of rooms"), ignoring location, size, condition, etc. - It's too simple to capture how prices actually work - It gives poor predictions even on the training data itself

docs.title: 3. Simple Analogy (Side-by-Side)
docs.text: Scenario Student Analogy Result Overfitting Memorized last year's exact exam paper, word-for-word Aces the old paper, fails the new one Underfitting Didn't study at all, doesn't know the basics Fails both old and new papers Good Fit (Ideal) Understood the actual concepts, not just memorized answers Does well on both old and new papers

docs.title: 4. Visual Way to Remember (Fitting a Line to Data)
docs.text:
Imagine plotting data points on a graph and trying to draw a line/curve through them:

  • Underfitting → A straight line that barely touches the pattern (too simple, misses obvious trends)
  • Good Fit → A smooth curve that follows the general trend of the data
  • Overfitting → A wiggly, zig-zag line that touches every single point exactly (too complex, follows noise instead of the trend)

Good Fit = capturing the "general shape" of the data, not the "exact dots."

docs.title: 5. How to Fix Overfitting
docs.text: Technique What It Does More training data Gives the model more variety to learn the real pattern, not memorize few examples Regularization Mathematical technique that discourages the model from becoming overly complex Dropout Randomly "turns off" some neurons during training so the model doesn't over-rely on specific patterns Early Stopping Stop training before the model starts memorizing instead of learning Simplify the Model Use a smaller/simpler model so it can't memorize too much detail

docs.title: 6. How to Fix Underfitting
docs.text: Technique What It Does More training time Let the model train longer to actually learn the patterns More complex model Use a bigger/more capable model that can capture the real pattern Better features Give the model more relevant input information (e.g., location + size + condition, not just rooms) Reduce regularization If regularization is too strict, it can prevent the model from learning enough

docs.title: 6. Key Terms (Quick Glossary)
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning Generalization The model's ability to perform well on new, unseen data (the real goal) Training Data Data used to teach the model Test/Validation Data New data used to check if the model actually learned properly Noise Random, irrelevant details in data that shouldn't be learned Regularization Techniques used to prevent overfitting by discouraging excessive complexity

docs.title: One-Line Summary (for quick revision)
docs.text:
• Overfitting → Model memorizes training data (including irrelevant noise) → great on training data, poor on new data.
  • Underfitting → Model is too simple/undertrained → poor on both training and new data.
  • Goal → A model that generalizes well — learns the real pattern, not memorized specifics.
  • Analogy → Overfitting = memorized last year's exam. Underfitting = didn't study at all. Good fit = actually understood the concept.

docs.title: Pre-training vs Fine-tuning
docs.text: Simple notes on the two main training stages that turn a raw neural network into a useful AI model like ChatGPT/Claude.

docs.title: Quick Overview
docs.text: Stage What Happens Goal Pre-training Model learns language/general knowledge from huge amounts of data Build a general "base" model that understands language Fine-tuning Pre-trained model is further trained on specific, smaller, focused data Make the model good at a specific task or behavior

docs.title: 1. Pre-training
docs.text:
Simple definition: The first, massive training stage where a model is trained on huge amounts of general text data (books, websites, articles, code, etc.) to learn language patterns, facts, grammar, and reasoning — from scratch.

  • Takes months and huge computing power (thousands of GPUs)
  • Uses general internet-scale data — not specific to any one task
  • Model learns: grammar, facts, how words relate, basic reasoning, coding patterns, etc.
  • Result: a "base model" — knows a lot, but isn't yet great at following instructions or being safe/helpful

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Think of pre-training like a person reading every book, article, and website on the internet for years — they come out knowing a huge amount about the world, language, and many topics, but they haven't been taught how to have a helpful, polite conversation yet.

This is the expensive, "from-scratch" stage. Only large companies (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta) usually do this, because it costs millions of dollars.

docs.title: 2. Fine-tuning
docs.text:
Simple definition: Taking an already pre-trained model and training it further on a smaller, specific dataset to make it better at a particular task, style, or behavior.

  • Much faster and cheaper than pre-training (hours/days, not months)
  • Uses smaller, focused datasets (e.g., customer support conversations, medical Q&A, coding examples)
  • Doesn't teach new "world knowledge" — it shapes behavior or specializes the model

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Take the same base model from pre-training (knows general language) and fine-tune it in different ways: - Fine-tune on customer support chats → becomes a great customer support bot - Fine-tune on medical Q&A data → becomes better at answering medical questions - Fine-tune on "being a helpful, safe assistant" conversations → becomes ChatGPT/Claude-like (this specific type is called instruction fine-tuning or RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)

Continuing the earlier analogy: after reading the whole internet (pre-training), the person now goes through a specific training program — like customer service training, or medical school — to specialize for a real job (fine-tuning).

docs.title: 3. Simple Analogy (Full Picture)
docs.text:
Think of becoming a doctor:

  1. Pre-training = Going through general schooling (school + college) — learning language, math, science, general knowledge broadly. Takes years.
  2. Fine-tuning = Going through medical school + specific specialization (e.g., becoming a cardiologist) — focused, shorter, specific training on top of your general knowledge.

You need the general foundation (pre-training) before the specific specialization (fine-tuning) makes sense.

docs.title: 4. Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text: Feature Pre-training Fine-tuning Data used Huge, general (internet-scale) Small, specific/focused Time & cost Very high (months, millions of $) Much lower (hours to days) Who does it Big AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) Big labs, and often businesses/developers too What it teaches General language, facts, reasoning Specific task, tone, style, or safety behavior Result A "base model" (raw capability) A specialized/refined model (ready for real use) Example Learning English + general world knowledge Learning to write like a legal assistant, or refuse harmful requests

docs.title: 5. Key Terms (Quick Glossary)
docs.text: Term Simple Meaning Base Model The raw model right after pre-training, before fine-tuning Instruction Fine-tuning Fine-tuning a model to follow instructions and have helpful conversations RLHF Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — a fine-tuning method where humans rate the model's answers to teach it what "good" responses look like Dataset The data used in either training stage Parameters The internal numbers of the model — pre-training sets most of them, fine-tuning adjusts them further

docs.title: Where This Fits
docs.text:
1. Pre-training  →  Base Model (knows language & facts, but raw/unrefined)
2. Fine-tuning   →  Refined Model (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude — helpful, safe, follows instructions)

docs.title: One-Line Summary (for quick revision)
docs.text:
• Pre-training → Teaching a model general language & knowledge using huge internet-scale data (expensive, from scratch).
  • Fine-tuning → Further training the model on smaller, specific data to specialize it or shape its behavior (cheaper, faster).
  • Analogy → Pre-training = general schooling. Fine-tuning = specialized professional training on top of that foundation.

docs.title: Prompt Engineering — Complete Notes (A to Z)
docs.text: Prompt Engineering = LLM ko sahi tareeke se instruction dene ki "art + science", taaki wo aapke desired output ko accurately, consistently aur efficiently generate kare. Simple words me: "Sawal sahi tareeke se poocho, jawab bhi accha milega."

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. What is Prompt Engineering
  2. Why Prompt Engineering Matters
  3. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
  4. Core Principles
  5. Prompting Techniques (Basic to Advanced)
  6. Prompt Frameworks (Templates)
  7. Advanced Reasoning Techniques
  8. Prompting for Different Tasks
  9. Common Mistakes to Avoid
  10. Prompt Evaluation & Iteration
  11. Security Concerns (Prompt Injection/Jailbreaking)
  12. Tools for Prompt Engineering
  13. Cheat Sheet / Quick Reference

docs.title: 1. What is Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Prompt = wo text/instruction jo aap LLM ko dete ho. Prompt Engineering = us instruction ko is tarah design karna ki LLM best possible, accurate, aur consistent output de.

Analogy: Socho ek naya intern hai jo bahut smart hai, lekin usse kaam samjhane ka tareeka clear hona chahiye — agar aap vague instruction doge ("kuch achha likh do"), toh result bhi vague aayega. Agar aap clear, structured instruction doge (context + task + format), toh result bhi sahi aayega.

docs.title: Why "Engineering"?
docs.text:
• Yeh sirf "achhi English likhna" nahi hai — isme systematic testing, iteration, aur structure hoti hai.
  • Same task ke liye alag-alag prompt phrasing se result bahut different aa sakta hai — isliye "engineer" karke best prompt dhoondhna padta hai.

docs.title: 2. Why Prompt Engineering Matters
docs.text:
Bina Prompt Engineering Sahi Prompt Engineering ke Saath Vague/generic answers Precise, targeted answers Inconsistent output format Consistent, structured output Hallucination zyada Hallucination kam (agar context diya jaye) Extra follow-up messages lagte hain Pehli baar me hi sahi result milta hai Model ki full capability use nahi hoti Model ki puri potential unlock hoti hai

Ek hi model (jaise Claude/GPT) ka output — sirf prompt badalne se — bahut different quality ka ho sakta hai. Isliye prompt engineering ek high-leverage skill hai.

docs.title: 3. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
docs.text:
Ek accha prompt usually in cheezon se milke banta hai:

Component Kya Hai Example Task/Instruction Aap kya chahte ho, clearly bolo "Summarize this article in 3 bullet points" Context Background info jo model ko chahiye "This is for a technical audience with ML background" Input Data Actual data/text jispe kaam karna hai The article text itself Output Format Answer kis format me chahiye "Respond in a JSON with keys: summary, key_points" Constraints/Rules Kya nahi karna chahiye "Don't use jargon", "Keep under 100 words" Examples (optional) Sample input-output pairs Few-shot examples (aage discuss karenge) Persona/Role (optional) Model ko kaunsa "role" nibhana hai "Act as a senior data scientist"

docs.title: Example — Bad vs Good Prompt
docs.text:
❌ Bad Prompt:

Write about AI.

(Too vague — length, tone, format, audience kuch bhi specify nahi)

✅ Good Prompt:

You are a technical writer for a beginner-friendly blog.
Write a 200-word explanation of "What is Artificial Intelligence?"
Use simple language, avoid jargon, and include one real-world example.
Format: 1 intro paragraph + 3 bullet points + 1 closing line.

docs.title: 4.1 Be Clear and Specific
docs.text:
• Vague instructions = vague output.
  • Explicitly state: what, how, format, length, tone.

docs.title: 4.2 Give Context
docs.text:
• Model ko background info do — audience, purpose, prior conversation.
  • Jitna zyada relevant context, utna accurate response.

docs.title: 4.3 Use Positive Instructions (batao kya karna hai, na ki sirf kya nahi karna)
docs.text:
• ❌ "Don't write a long answer" (vague — kitna lamba "long" hai?)
  • ✅ "Write in exactly 3 sentences"

docs.title: 4.4 Specify Output Format
docs.text:
• JSON, table, bullet points, markdown, specific structure — jo bhi chahiye, clearly bolo.
  • Yeh especially important hai jab output ko programmatically use karna ho (e.g., API response parsing).

docs.title: 4.5 Break Complex Tasks into Steps
docs.text: • Ek hi bade complex task ke bajaye, usko chhote steps me todo (chaining), ya model ko khud step-by-step sochne ko kaho (Chain-of-Thought — aage discuss).

docs.title: 4.6 Use Examples (Show, Don't Just Tell)
docs.text:
• Agar format/style specific hai, toh 1-2 example de do (few-shot prompting).
  • Examples se model pattern jaldi samajhta hai instructions se zyada.

docs.title: 4.7 Iterate and Test
docs.text:
• Pehli baar me perfect prompt kam hi milta hai.
  • Test karo, output dekho, prompt refine karo — yeh ek loop hai.

docs.title: 4.8 Assign a Role/Persona
docs.text: • "Act as an expert X" — isse model ka tone, depth, aur vocabulary us role ke hisaab se adjust hota hai.

docs.title: 4.9 Use Delimiters
docs.text:
• Input text ko clearly mark karo (quotes, triple backticks, XML tags) taaki model confuse na ho ki instruction kya hai aur data kya hai.
Summarize the text between triple backticks:

[article text here]

docs.title: 4.10 Encourage Step-by-Step Reasoning
docs.text: • Complex/logical tasks ke liye: "Think step by step before answering" — isse accuracy badh jati hai (especially math, logic, multi-step problems me).

docs.title: 5.1 Zero-Shot Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Bina kisi example ke, seedha task de do. Model apne pre-trained knowledge se hi answer deta hai.

Prompt: "Classify the sentiment of this review as Positive, Negative, or Neutral: 
'The product broke after two days, very disappointed.'"
  • ✅ Quick, simple tasks ke liye.
  • ❌ Complex/niche format chahiye ho toh kaafi nahi hota.

docs.title: 5.2 Few-Shot Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Task se pehle 2-5 examples do (input → output pairs), taaki model pattern samajh jaye.

Prompt:
Review: "Amazing quality, will buy again!" → Sentiment: Positive
Review: "Terrible experience, item was broken." → Sentiment: Negative
Review: "It's okay, does the job." → Sentiment: Neutral

Review: "Best purchase this year!" → Sentiment: ?
  • ✅ Specific format/style enforce karne ke liye best hai.
  • ✅ Model ko naye/unseen tasks ke patterns samjhane me help karta hai.
  • ❌ Prompt lamba ho jata hai (more tokens = more cost).

docs.title: 5.3 Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Model ko boलो ki step-by-step socho, seedha final answer mat do.

Prompt: "A store had 120 apples. They sold 45 in the morning and 30 in the afternoon. 
How many are left? Think step by step."

Model Output:
Step 1: Start with 120 apples.
Step 2: Sold 45 in morning → 120 - 45 = 75
Step 3: Sold 30 in afternoon → 75 - 30 = 45
Final Answer: 45 apples left.
  • ✅ Math, logic, multi-step reasoning tasks me accuracy bahut improve hoti hai.
  • ✅ Errors trace karna aasan ho jata hai (aap dekh sakte ho model kahan galat socha).
  • ❌ Response lamba ho jata hai, thoda slow/costly.

Trigger phrase: "Let's think step by step" — yeh simple line accuracy ko dramatically improve kar sakti hai complex tasks me.

docs.title: 5.4 Self-Consistency
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Same question ko multiple baar (different reasoning paths se) solve karwao, phir majority vote se final answer nikaalo.

  • Model se ek hi problem ke 5 alag-alag CoT solutions generate karwao.

  • Jo answer sabse zyada baar aaya, wahi final answer maano.

  • ✅ Accuracy aur reliability badhti hai, especially tricky reasoning problems me.

  • ❌ Multiple API calls chahiye — cost/time zyada lagta hai.

docs.title: 5.5 Role Prompting (Persona-Based)
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Model ko ek specific "role/persona" assign karo — expert, teacher, critic, etc.

Prompt: "You are a senior cybersecurity expert with 15 years of experience. 
Explain SQL injection to a junior developer in simple terms."
  • ✅ Tone, depth, vocabulary automatically us role ke hisaab se adjust ho jaate hain.
  • ✅ Creative writing, expert advice, roleplay scenarios ke liye useful.

docs.title: 5.6 Instruction Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Bas directly, clearly instruction do — bina kisi role/example ke, seedha kaam bata do.

Prompt: "Translate the following sentence into French: 'How are you today?'"
  • ✅ Simple, direct tasks ke liye best — jab task itself hi clear ho.

docs.title: 5.7 Contextual Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Task se pehle relevant background/context provide karo, taaki response us context ke according tailor ho.

Prompt: "Our company sells eco-friendly packaging to small businesses. 
Write a tagline that emphasizes sustainability and affordability."
  • ✅ Business, marketing, personalized content ke liye zaroori.

docs.title: 5.8 Iterative/Refinement Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Ek hi response ko baar-baar refine karo follow-up prompts se.

Prompt 1: "Write a short bio for a software engineer."
Prompt 2 (follow-up): "Make it more casual and add a fun fact about hobbies."
Prompt 3 (follow-up): "Now shorten it to 2 sentences."
  • ✅ Complex/nuanced outputs ke liye — ek hi baar me perfect prompt likhne ki jagah, step-by-step refine karo.

docs.title: 5.9 Negative Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Model ko batao ki kya avoid karna hai (image generation models me zyada common, text models me bhi useful).

Prompt: "Write a product description. Do NOT use words like 'revolutionary', 
'game-changing', or excessive exclamation marks."
  • ✅ Specific unwanted patterns/words/style se bachne ke liye.

docs.title: 5.10 Meta Prompting
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Model se hi poocho ki "is task ke liye best prompt kya hoga" — yaani prompt banane ke liye khud LLM ka use karna.

Prompt: "I want to build a prompt that makes an LLM summarize legal documents 
accurately without missing key clauses. Write the best possible prompt for this task."
  • ✅ Jab khud prompt likhna mushkil lage, model se hi help lo.

docs.title: 6. Prompt Frameworks (Ready-Made Templates)
docs.text: Yeh frameworks structure dete hain — kaunsa element kis order me daalna hai.

docs.title: 6.1 RTF Framework (Role — Task — Format)
docs.text:
Role: You are a [role].
Task: [What to do]
Format: [Desired output format]

Example:

Role: You are an experienced fitness coach.
Task: Create a 7-day beginner workout plan.
Format: Present as a table with columns: Day, Exercise, Sets/Reps, Rest Time.

docs.title: 6.2 CRISPE Framework
docs.text:
• Capacity/Role — Model kaunsa role play kare
  • Request — Kya karna hai
  • Insight — Context/background info
  • Statement — Constraints/rules
  • Personality — Tone/style
  • Experiment — Multiple variations try karna

docs.title: 6.3 CO-STAR Framework
docs.text:
• Context — Background
  • Objective — Task ka goal
  • Style — Writing style
  • Tone — Emotional tone
  • Audience — Kaun padhega
  • Response Format — Output structure

docs.title: 6.4 TAG Framework (Task — Action — Goal)
docs.text:
Task: [What needs to be done]
Action: [Steps to take]
Goal: [Desired outcome]

Tip: Framework koi bhi use karo, key idea same hai — Role + Context + Task + Format + Constraints ko systematically cover karna.

docs.title: 7.1 Tree of Thought (ToT)
docs.text:
Simple Meaning: Chain-of-Thought ka advanced version — ek hi linear path ke bajaye, model multiple possible reasoning paths (branches) explore karta hai, phir best path choose karta hai.

  • Complex problem-solving, planning tasks, puzzles ke liye best.
  • Model different approaches try karta hai aur unme se best evaluate karke aage badhta hai (jaise ek decision tree).

docs.title: 7.2 ReAct (Reasoning + Acting)
docs.text:
